name: Wrangell-St. Elias National Park
line: Kennecott mill town and the Root Glacier

jewels.name: Kennecott Mines National Historic Landmark
jewels.booking_route: none needed - the park charges no entrance fee
jewels.blurb: "Kennecott is considered the best remaining example of early 20th Century copper mining"; "From 1911 to 1938, nearly $200 million worth of copper was processed." Listed on the National Register in 1978, a National Historic Landmark since 1986; exhibits in the General Store, the North Sacking Shed and the General Manager's Office.

jewels.name: Root Glacier Trail
jewels.blurb: "Of the 5,000 square miles of glacial ice in Wrangell-St. Elias, the Root Glacier is the most accessible. A moderate 1 1/2 mile walk from the historic mining town of Kennecott along the Root Glacier Trail leads you onto the glacier. Be aware that glaciers can be dangerous."

jewels.name: Kennecott Mill Town Tour (St. Elias Alpine Guides)
jewels.blurb: "St. Elias Alpine Guides holds the exclusive concession with the National Park Service, and access to the 14-story Concentration Mill is only possible through this tour." Two hours, about a mile; adult (13+) $36, child (12-) $18; "All ages welcome"; "ADVANCED RESERVATIONS STRONGLY ENCOURAGED!"

jewels.name: Wrangell Mountain Air flightseeing
jewels.booking_route: request form and email on the own website
jewels.blurb: McCarthy-based since 1992; "all flightsees originate from and return to McCarthy, and there is a two person minimum". Mile High Cliff Tour "50 minute - $330/person"; Thirteen Glacier Tour "70 minute - $405/person" over the Nizina, Chitistone Canyon and the University Range.

jewels.name: Kennicott Wilderness Guides glacier hikes
jewels.blurb: Half-Day Glacier Hike (5 hours), Full-Day (7-8 hours), Ice Explorer Climb & Hike - "Great for families with mixed abilities" - fly-in hikes and Donoho Falls; trips include "Round-trip transportation from your local lodging" and "Any technical, or glacier gear required for the hike." "Currently booking trips for 2026!"

jewels.name: St. Elias Alpine Guides multi-day Group Trips
jewels.booking_route: own website online booking or a call with the Expedition Coordinator; deposit, balance 30 days before
jewels.blurb: "the oldest continuously operating business in Wrangell-St. Elias National Park", guiding "since 1978". Set-date Group Trips - basecamp hiking, backpacking, rafting, mountaineering - that "max out at 8 participants and 12 participants for rafting trips"; "We'll run the trip even if only 1 person signs up!"; trip packages arrange "transportation to and from the Wrangells, local lodging". FAQ: "Limited rental equipment is available to our multi-day trip guests."

jewels.name: Kennicott Wilderness Guides Package Trips
jewels.blurb: "two, three, and five-day itineraries": Water & Ice (2 days), Water, Ice & Air (3 days, adds a scenic flight to a fly-in hike), Water, Ice & Basecamp (5 days, "3 days of basecamping"). "Each trip includes a private guide, prepared lunches, and flexible scheduling"; "Transportation to McCarthy-Kennicott and lodging are not included."

jewels.name: Wrangell Mountain Air Chitina-McCarthy flights and Glacier Adventure Day Trip
jewels.booking_route: request form on the own website
jewels.blurb: Scheduled flights leave Chitina 9:05a and McCarthy 5:00p. Glacier Adventure Day Trip (flight plus a half-day Root Glacier hike with a St. Elias Alpine guide and a Kennicott Glacier Lodge sack lunch) "$ 590 /person (includes excise tax)"; Packrafting Adventure Day Trip with Kennicott Wilderness Guides "$ 780 /person"; children 12 and under $20 off.

jewels.name: Copper Valley Air Service
jewels.blurb: Year-round from Glennallen: "Flightseeing tours of Wrangell St. Elias National Park. Mail plane flights or scheduled service between Anchorage, Glennallen, and McCarthy"; listed at "Flightseeing $350+ | Air Taxi $450+ One Way". Its own site did not resolve when fetched; sourced to the Alaska.org listing.

jewels.name: Ma Johnson's Historic Hotel
jewels.blurb: "Pete & Ma Johnson's restored boarding house" in McCarthy; "There are 20 rooms in Ma Johnson's"; rooms carry "Luxury Linens", robes, breakfast and a "Complimentary Copper Town Shuttle Pass - NPS authorized transportation". The lodge calls it "the only authentic historic hotel in the park."

jewels.name: Kennicott Glacier Lodge
jewels.blurb: In Kennecott itself: the Main Lodge (built 1987) has "a 190-foot-long front porch" and 23 rooms with shared baths; the South Wing's 20 rooms each have a private bath and two queens; breakfast buffet, lunch from a menu, "dinner at a single seating with a fixed menu." Own site refused the fetch (HTTP 403); sourced to Alaska.org.

jewels.name: Ultima Thule Lodge
jewels.booking_route: reservations page on the own website; info@ultimathulelodge.com
jewels.blurb: "an adventure centric wilderness outpost inside the vast Wrangell/St. Elias Mountains", "a hundred miles from paved roads", on a glacier river inside the park; bush-plane adventures; "stays are available May-September"; "a haven for small groups and intimate gatherings" with Whole Package private-use reservations.

jewels.name: Copper River Princess Wilderness Lodge
jewels.blurb: 85 rooms on 200 acres "near the junction of the Klutina and Copper Rivers", "just four miles from the Wrangell-St. Elias National Park visitor's center"; the Two Rivers Restaurant; a Guest Service Desk books Gulkana River rafting and Kennicott visits; Princess sells it inside Alaska vacation packages.

jewels.name: Old Town Copper Center Inn & Restaurant
jewels.booking_route: Book Now on the own website; (907) 822-3245
jewels.blurb: Traces its roots to "the original Copper Center Lodge, established in 1896 along Alaska's historic Richardson Trail"; the original lodge was "lost to fire" in 2012 and "historic outbuildings remain". Guest rooms plus Nummy's Restaurant; "Minutes from Wrangell-St. Elias National Park".

jewels.name: Lancaster's Backpacker Hotel
jewels.blurb: McCarthy Lodge's budget house: "budget-friendly accommodations with shared bathrooms, basic amenities, and a casual, social atmosphere, ideal for backpackers"; private rooms for one to four, breakfast at McCarthy Lodge and the Copper Town Shuttle pass included.

jewels.name: Base Camp Kennicott
jewels.booking_route: no reservation; check in with the camp host
jewels.blurb: At "Mile 59.4 McCarthy Road End" by the footbridge: "Uncrowded, Open Camping Sites - Tents/Cars/Trailers/RVs (no hook-ups)"; open "MAY 21 through Sept 30, 2026"; 2026 rates: 24-hour parking $12, basic camping $35, oversize (over 25 feet) $45; "RESERVATIONS ARE NOT REQUIRED."

jewels.name: Tolsona Wilderness Campground
jewels.blurb: Glennallen: "RV sites equipped with water and 30 or 50 amp electric hook-ups", creekside tent sites, bathrooms, showers, laundry, dump station, yurts that "have electric, heat and can sleep up to six people" (no bedding), three group sites "for up to 15 RVs", themed weekends and a playground. Booked on Campspot.

jewels.name: Northern Nights Campground & RV Park
jewels.blurb: Mile Post 188.7 Glenn Highway, Glennallen: 28 wooded RV sites (5 full hook-up, 16 pull-thru), 5 dry tent sites, "RV sites are 50- 60 +feet in length" with some 70-90 feet, showers, laundry, free Wi-Fi; "2025 Marks our 35th season!"

jewels.name: Kendesnii Campground
jewels.booking_route: none - first come, first served; no reservations taken
jewels.blurb: "the only National Park Service campground in the park" at Mile 27.8 Nabesna Road: 10 sites, each with a picnic table and fire ring, "can accommodate a small to medium RV"; "free and open year-round. No reservations are required and none are taken." Canoeing, waterfowl and grayling fishing.

jewels.name: Public-use cabins
jewels.booking_route: NPS email form for the four reservable cabins
jewels.blurb: "All cabins are remote and very rustic"; "Most cabins are accessible only by flying into remote airstrips." Viking Lodge, Caribou Creek, Nugget Creek and Esker Stream "are the only cabins that require reservations"; the rest are first come, first served. "The park does not stock: firewood, water, dishes, supplies, sleeping pads, bedding".

jewels.name: Wrangell-St. Elias Visitor Center and Ahtna Cultural Center, Copper Center
jewels.blurb: Mile 106.8 Richardson Highway, "about 10 miles south of the intersection of the Glenn Highway and the Richardson Highway in Glennallen": film, exhibits, a short trail, the park store. In the same complex the Ahtna Cultural Center, "Operated by Ahtna, Incorporated", shows "a beautifully hand-built fish wheel". 2026 hours May 11 - September 20, 9-5.

jewels.name: Junior Ranger and ranger programmes
jewels.booking_route: none needed - free; booklets at any visitor center
jewels.blurb: "Throughout the summer months, park rangers present free interpretive talks, guided walks, and evening programs. The Junior Ranger program is available too! This is a free program for kids of all ages"; a Junior Ranger Angler booklet too. Weekend evening programmes at the Kennecott Recreation Hall.

jewels.name: Kennecott Visitor Center
jewels.blurb: "located in the historic Blackburn School within the Kennecott Mill Town", "5 miles north from McCarthy": exhibits, park film in the General Store, ranger programmes, an Alaska Geographic bookstore, backcountry trip planning. 2026 hours May 23 - September 13, daily 9-5; closed fall to spring.

jewels.name: McCarthy Road
jewels.blurb: "a narrow, gravel road that is 59 miles to the Kennicott River Bridge" on the old Copper River & Northwestern Railway route: "Drive slow. Be aware of soft road edges, potholes, and railroad ties and possible spikes." It is "owned and operated by the State of Alaska". Free day parking at the State Wayside (mile 55) or the McCarthy Road Information Station (mile 58.6).

jewels.name: Nabesna Road
jewels.booking_route: none needed - public road; first come, first served pullouts
jewels.blurb: From mile 60 of the Tok Cutoff, "nestled in a valley between two mountain ranges": a "gravel road that is 42 miles long, with 3 stream crossings"; pullout campsites at Rufus Creek, Kettle Lake, Dead Dog Hill, Rock Lake and Jack Creek, where "you may be able to view Dall Sheep." No fuel in Slana or on the road.

jewels.name: Bonanza Mine and Jumbo Mine trails
jewels.blurb: From Kennecott: Bonanza Mine Trail, "Strenuous day hike to tremendous views and remnants of the Bonanza Mine bunkhouse"; Jumbo Mine Trail, "Strenuous day hike to panoramic views and remnants of the Jumbo Mine bunkhouse."

jewels.name: Erie Mine Trail (partly washed out)
jewels.blurb: "Hike on a primitive trail alongside the Root Glacier for 4 miles (one way)" toward the Erie Mine cables and the Stairway Icefall. ⚠️ NPS: "Update fall 2023: A landslide has washed out a significant portion of the trail several miles in. This point has been marked with signage and travel beyond it is not recommended." The Erie Mine Trail food box "was REMOVED".

jewels.name: Crystalline Hills Trail
jewels.blurb: McCarthy Road Mile 34.8: "2.5 mile loop", "2-3 hours", "Easy to Moderate", "Road access, beautiful views"; "bug spray is highly recommended in summer."

jewels.name: Donoho Basin and Jumbo Creek backcountry camping
jewels.booking_route: none - group registration at a visitor center or wrst_backcountry@nps.gov
jewels.blurb: Jumbo Creek, "1.4 miles north by trail past Kennecott mill town", primitive NPS camping with bear boxes; Donoho Basin, 3-6 miles north, where a group "of more than 8 people, maximum 12" must register with the park. "This route requires glacier travel experience and equipment."

jewels.name: Sport hunting in the national preserve
jewels.booking_route: Alaska state licence; a registered guide where required
jewels.blurb: "Sport hunting is ONLY allowed within the NATIONAL PRESERVE and must be conducted in accordance with Alaska State Law"; "An Alaska state hunting license is required for all hunters age 16 or older"; registered guides operate under permit, from "private fly-in lodging facilities" to "basic 'spike' camp operations accessible by horseback."

jewels.name: Bear-resistant food container
jewels.blurb: "Bear Resistant Food Containers (BRFC) are required for all backcountry camping". "You need to buy or rent a BRFC for your backcountry trip prior to your arrival at the park"; there is "a limited amount to borrow at the Visitor Centers and Ranger Stations". Each "holds enough food for one person for about 5 days".

jewels.name: Crampons or ice spikes for the Root Glacier
jewels.blurb: NPS on the Root Glacier: "It is recommended to wear crampons or ice spikes on your shoes and go with an experienced guide." On a guided hike the guide supplies them: St. Elias Alpine Guides "do not rent out crampons" but include them on glacier tours.

jewels.name: Satellite communicator for the backcountry
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Satellite phones and satellite messengers are the only way to communicate from the backcountry of Wrangell-St. Elias. We recommend bringing a satellite communication device"; "In an emergency, help will not be immediate".

jewels.name: Bear spray, bought before you fly
jewels.blurb: NPS gear list: "Bear spray - Note that this cannot be carried on planes or trains. Bear spray is permitted in the United States when crossing the land border by vehicle." Canada admits bear spray that carries USEPA on the label.

jewels.name: Layers, trekking poles and bug spray - no gear store at the end of the road
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Plan on temps ranging from as warm as 75 F to as cold as 20 F, possibly in the same day!"; it lists trekking poles, a tent ("We strongly discourage bivy sacks") and bug spray, and warns "Do not count on acquiring or renting gear once you arrive at the park." St. Elias Alpine Guides confirms "there is no gear store in McCarthy-Kennecott".

jewels.name: Salmon & Bear Restaurant
jewels.booking_route: reservation form on the own website
jewels.blurb: McCarthy Lodge's dining room: "Wine Spectator Award Of Excellence each year Since 2020"; "just 10 intimate tables" that "sells out most busy summer nights"; local ingredients "like our wild caught Copper River Red Salmon"; breakfast 7-9 am, dinner 5:30-9 pm.

jewels.name: The Golden Saloon
jewels.booking_route: reservation form on the own website
jewels.blurb: "the center of evening entertainment in Wrangell St. Elias National Park": buffalo burgers, wings, salads, wine flights and single malts; lunch and dinner noon to midnight. Alaska.org: "Thursday evenings are open mic night in McCarthy".

jewels.name: Roadside Potatohead
jewels.blurb: "Quirky restaurant and espresso bar that serves great burritos and burgers on the outskirts of town", Kennicott Road, McCarthy; 907-554-4440. No own site found; sourced to Alaska.org.

jewels.name: Kennicott Glacier Lodge dining room
jewels.blurb: "Breakfast is served as a buffet, lunch is served from a menu, and dinner at a single seating with a fixed menu. The 'wilderness gourmet' dishes feature homemade soups, pastries, breads, and delicious desserts." Its sack lunches ride on the Wrangell Mountain Air day trips.

jewels.name: Nummy's Restaurant, Old Town Copper Center
jewels.blurb: "In 1948, Nummy's Restaurant began serving guests and quickly became a local favorite"; "hearty breakfasts, delicious lunches, and homestyle dinners in a relaxed Alaskan atmosphere."

jewels.name: Two Rivers Restaurant, Copper River Princess
jewels.blurb: "a two-level dining area with excellent mountain and valley views"; "our Two Rivers Restaurant provides excellent mountain and valley views alongside signature Alaska cuisine."

jewels.name: Caribou Grill, Glennallen
jewels.blurb: Listed by the Copper Valley Chamber of Commerce - the body the NPS sends visitors to for area restaurants - under Glennallen: "Caribou Grill - (907) 822-4222". Nothing else about it is stated here.

jewels.name: McCarthy
jewels.blurb: McCarthy Lodge calls it "the Gateway Community to America's largest national park", with "Open Mic Thursday's, Live Music on Friday and Saturday nights." The NPS: the town "is located 1/2 mile east" of the Kennicott River Bridge, and "There are no services available in McCarthy or Kennecott during the winter."

jewels.name: McCarthy/Kennicott Museum
jewels.blurb: In the old railway depot: the copper rush "between 1900 and 1938", with "pictures of railway construction - 196 miles of track from Cordova". Sourced to Alaska.org; no own site found.

jewels.name: Alaska Overlander rooftop-tent rigs
jewels.blurb: Anchorage-based rentals that Alaska.org lists for the McCarthy Road: "Complete with rooftop tents that set up in minutes, camp stove, and refrigerator"; "Season: April to Mid-October", "$299+ per day", "3+ days". Alaska.org notes "many Alaska car rental companies don't allow their vehicles on non-paved roads" and that this one does.

faq.q: Do you need tickets for Wrangell-St. Elias National Park and Preserve?
faq.a: No entrance ticket is needed. The NPS states: "Wrangell-St. Elias National Park & Preserve is one of the National Park Service sites that does NOT charge an entrance fee." Private businesses may charge for parking and camping.

faq.q: How big is Wrangell-St. Elias National Park?
faq.a: The NPS: "It is the largest national park in the United States, with a size equal to six Yellowstone National Parks", and the park and preserve contain "approximately 13 million acres of public land in south-central Alaska."

faq.q: Can you drive to Wrangell-St. Elias National Park?
faq.a: Yes, on two State-owned gravel roads. "The McCarthy Road is a narrow, gravel road that is 59 miles to the Kennicott River Bridge"; "There is no public vehicle access to Kennecott Mill town", 5 miles beyond McCarthy, and "most rental car companies do not allow their cars on this road." The Nabesna Road in the north is 42 miles of gravel with 3 stream crossings.

faq.q: How far is Wrangell-St. Elias National Park from Anchorage?
faq.a: The NPS gives drive time, not mileage: "Kennecott Mines National Historic Landmark is located approximately 8 hours (by car) from Anchorage" - east on the Glenn Highway, south on the Richardson, east on the Edgerton, then 59 miles on the McCarthy Road.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Wrangell-St. Elias National Park?
faq.a: "Summer is the primary season for visiting Wrangell-St. Elias from mid-May through mid-September. Winter arrives early to interior Alaska and by the end of September, available services and facilities are limited." Visitor centers and ranger stations close from October through April.

faq.q: Can you camp in Wrangell-St. Elias National Park?
faq.a: Yes. Kendesnii Campground on the Nabesna Road "is the only National Park Service campground in the park": 10 sites, "free and open year-round. No reservations are required and none are taken." Pullouts along the Nabesna Road and primitive NPS areas north of Kennecott are also available.

faq.q: Can you hunt in Wrangell-St. Elias National Park?
faq.a: Only in the preserve: "Sport hunting is ONLY allowed within the NATIONAL PRESERVE and must be conducted in accordance with Alaska State Law. Subsistence hunting by qualified, local rural residents is authorized in both the park and preserve." An Alaska state licence is required from age 16.

faq.q: When was Wrangell-St. Elias National Park established?
faq.a: "When the park and preserve were established by the U.S. Congress in 1980". The NPS dates the act that created it, the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act, to "December 2, 1980".

faq.q: What can you do at Wrangell-St. Elias National Park?
faq.a: At Kennecott the NPS lists day hikes - the Root Glacier, Jumbo Mine and Bonanza Mine trails - and the mill town tour by the concessioner, "the only way to see inside the Concentration Mill building and the Leaching Plant"; rangers give free talks, walks and a Junior Ranger programme in summer.

seo.meta_title: Wrangell-St. Elias National Park: Kennecott & Root Glacier | TravelWell
seo.meta_description: The largest US national park: free entry, the Kennecott mill town, the Root Glacier, 59 miles of gravel McCarthy Road, and where to camp, stay and fly nearby.

name: Katmai National Park
line: Brooks Falls brown bears and a volcanic valley

jewels.name: Brooks Falls Platform and Brooks Falls Trail
jewels.booking_route: none needed - no entrance fee; reached by floatplane or water taxi to Brooks Camp
jewels.blurb: "This is the most popular trail in Katmai": 1.2 mi, easy, wheelchair accessible; "At the end of the trail, two raised platforms offer a bird's eye view of bears fishing in the Brooks River. Bear viewing at the Falls is best during the July salmon run." The Falls Platform "has a maximum capacity of 40 people"; when full, rangers keep a waiting list and visitors may be asked to yield after one hour.

jewels.name: Brooks Camp bear orientation ("Bear School")
jewels.booking_route: none needed - given at the Brooks Camp Visitor Center on arrival
jewels.blurb: "All visitors to Brooks Camp are required to begin their stay by attending a brief bear safety talk outlining park regulations." The rules: "Remain at least 50 yards (46 meters) from any bear at all times"; "Never run from any bear"; outside designated areas "you cannot possess any food (even gum and candy) or beverages other than plain water"; "No clothing, bags, or other equipment can be left unattended at any time."

jewels.name: Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes Tour
jewels.booking_route: reservations at Brooks Lodge or through Katmailand, Inc. (1-800-544-0551)
jewels.blurb: "Not far from Brooks River, the largest volcanic eruption of the 20th century began on June 6, 1912." A day-long tour: 46-mile bus trip from the South Platform at 9 a.m. daily June 7 to September 17, lunch at the Robert F. Griggs Visitor Center, then an optional ranger-led hike of "3.4 miles (5.4 km) round trip with 1000 feet (305 m) of elevation change"; 7 hours. "A fee is charged for this tour and reservations are required."

jewels.name: Brooks Camp Campground
jewels.blurb: The only designated campground in Katmai, "surrounded by an electric fence to deter bears from entering. The fence is bear-resistant, but not bear-proof." Three covered cooking shelters, a food and gear cache, fuel lockers, two vault toilets, potable water June 1 through September 18. $18 per person per night June 1-September 17, $10 in May and from September 18 to October 31; "Group size is limited to 6"; Access and Senior Pass holders 50% off (card holder only).

jewels.name: Brooks Lodge
jewels.booking_route: Katmailand lottery application (katmailand.com/brooks-lodge-lottery/), then a 50% deposit within 3 days
jewels.blurb: "The Only Full-Service Lodge Within Walking Distance of Brooks Falls": sixteen rooms, "each with private facilities", each with "2 sets of bunk beds that can accommodate up to four guests". Rooms are allocated by lottery: "Due to a high demand for overnight accommodations at Brooks, we operate a random lottery system". 2026 season June 1-September 18.

jewels.name: Katmai Air - Brooks Falls day tour from Anchorage
jewels.blurb: "A One Day Adventure to the World Famous Brooks Falls": an "approx. one hour and fifteen minute flight from Anchorage to King Salmon", then a "scenic 20-minute flight to Brooks Lodge" by float plane; "As a sister operation of Brooks Lodge, we're proud to say we offer the most dependable day trip option to Brooks from Anchorage." June 1-September 18, 2026, $1489 per person including taxes and fees.

jewels.name: Riffles and Lower River platforms
jewels.booking_route: none needed - free at Brooks Camp
jewels.blurb: "Five elevated viewing platforms at Brooks Camp are the only outdoor locations where bears can be safely observed at close distances." "Neither the Riffles nor the three Lower River platforms have a time limit or capacity, and they can offer just as many rewarding bear viewing opportunities as Brooks Falls." On the platforms "please keep your voices low and avoid cheering for bears" and turn camera flash off.

jewels.name: Katmai Water Taxi
jewels.blurb: "Your Gateway to Katmai": a shuttle from your location in King Salmon to Lake Camp Boat Launch, then "a 45-minute ride across Naknek Lake to Brooks Camp. The water taxi departs every odd hour from 7 AM to 5 PM. Upon arrival, our crew will guide you to the Visitor Center for the bear viewing orientation." $205 per one-way ticket, "CUA fee included in the price". Season ended; "2027 bookings will be available in late November or December 2026."

jewels.name: Smokey Bay Air - Katmai coast bear viewing from Homer
jewels.booking_route: own website Book Online (50% deposit or pay in full) or 907-531-0602
jewels.blurb: "You will be accompanied by an experienced bush pilot who will be your bear viewing guide. Your plane will land on one of the National Park beaches, just a short walk away from the main attraction: brown bears in their natural habitat." About five hours - "approximately one hour flight each way and three hours on the beach"; "a 280 pound limit per person and a 7 year old minimum age"; $1145.00 per person (2 person min.), "Price includes all National Park fees". 2100 Kachemak Drive, Homer; 907-531-0602.

jewels.name: Beluga Air - Katmai bear viewing from Homer
jewels.blurb: "Since 1984": "Daily tours to Katmai National Park to view majestic Alaska Coastal Brown Bears in the wild." Its most popular tour: "guided June hikes. We specialize in small-group tours led by expert naturalists". Also McNeil River Bear Sanctuary transport for permit winners. info@belugaair.com, (907) 235-8256.

jewels.name: Regal Air - Katmai bear viewing from Anchorage
jewels.blurb: "Your Katmai Bear Viewing Adventure Begins when you depart Anchorage on one of our aircraft and head south along the Cook Inlet." By floatplane direct or twin-engine then floatplane, "Both options take approximately 2.5 hours each way", with "(Approximately 4 hours)" on the ground; after "a quick bear orientation with one of the park rangers", "approximately 2 miles of easy walking" to a platform. (907) 243-8535.

jewels.name: Hallo Bay
jewels.booking_route: none needed in the park - reached by an authorized air taxi
jewels.blurb: "Hallo Bay sits on the Pacific Coast of Katmai in the shadow of Kukak Volcano"; "Most commonly in June, bears roam about feasting on the nutrient dense sedges. Other wildlife in Halo Bay include wolves, foxes, and migratory birds." Reached by air taxi from King Salmon, Homer, Kodiak or Anchorage; "The core meadow areas of Hallo Bay are closed to camping from April 1st through October 31st".

jewels.name: Fishing the Brooks River and Katmai waters
jewels.booking_route: none needed in the park - an Alaska sport fishing license (ADF&G); a Brooks River Corridor permit ($6 Recreation.gov booking fee) applies June 15-October 31
jewels.blurb: Rainbow trout, arctic char, dolly varden, arctic grayling, lake trout and five Pacific salmon species; "An Alaska sport fishing license is required of all nonresidents 16 and over and most residents 16 to 59." At Brooks: "Fishing must be terminated within 50 yards of any bear—no lures can remain in the water. When playing a fish, always be prepared to break your fishing line in case a bear approaches."

jewels.name: Dumpling Mountain Trail
jewels.blurb: 1.5 mi, moderate to strenuous: "climbs 800 feet (244 m) over 1.5 miles (2.4 km) to an overlook above Brooks Camp with expansive views of Naknek Lake, Brooks River, and Lake Brooks." The trailhead is in the campground; the summit (2440 ft) is "another 2.5 mi (4 km) beyond the overlook", through "boreal forest, subalpine meadows, and alpine tundra."

jewels.name: Grosvenor Lodge
jewels.blurb: Inside Katmai, "at the confluence between two lakes, Lake Coville and Lake Grosvenor"; "Limited to no more than six guests at a time, Grosvenor provides the 'it feels like my own Alaska fishing lodge' experience and is ideal for families, business associates, and/or a close group of fishing buddies." 3-, 4- and 7-night trips June 7-September 27, transfer days Wednesday and Sunday, flights not included.

jewels.name: Kulik Lodge
jewels.blurb: "Established in 1950, Kulik Lodge is recognized as Alaska's first fly-out fishing lodge. Located in the heart of Katmai National Park and Preserve". Listed by the NPS among lodges within the park.

jewels.name: King Salmon Lodge
jewels.blurb: "An Alaska Fishing Lodge where family and friends create memories of a lifetime", "ideally situated on the scenic Naknek River"; it offers "King Salmon Lodge Bear Tours" and guided fishing. Natural Habitat Adventures describes it as "rustic luxury on the edge of Katmai National Park" with the Brooks River "just 15 minutes away by floatplane".

jewels.name: Brooks Lodge dining room
jewels.booking_route: purchased ahead through Katmailand or on-site
jewels.blurb: "Hearty Alaska fare is served buffet style each day for breakfast, lunch, and dinner in the lodge dining area. Cocktails are also available for purchase at the lodge bar each afternoon and evening." 2026 buffets: breakfast $25, lunch $45, dinner $52 (adult); child prices for ages 2-11; "Senior discounts also available." Open to day visitors.

jewels.name: The Katmai Trading Post
jewels.blurb: Katmailand's store at Brooks: "Canoes, kayaks, chest waders, Swarovski binoculars, and single burner stoves available for rent. Bear resistant containers, showers, and towels also available for campers"; camp stove fuel ("White gas, propane, & Jetboil fuel"), insect repellent, fishing tackle and Alaska fishing licenses. 2026: chest waders $40/day, Swarovski binoculars $30/day, canoe or single kayak $50/day.

jewels.name: Bear-resistant food container for the backcountry
jewels.blurb: NPS: "The use of bear-resistant food containers (BRFCs) is mandatory in all backcountry areas. A limited supply of BRFCs are available to borrow free of charge at the visitor centers in King Salmon and Brooks Camp." It also recommends "an electric fence when camping in the wilderness. As a reminder, electric fences are bear deterrents; they are not bear proof."

jewels.name: Bear spray for Katmai's trails and coast
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Use your bear spray if you think the bear will attack. While most charges stop short of contact, there is no way to know and bear spray is a very effective tool to stop a charge." With a non-defensive bear: "shout, make yourself look large and threatening, throw a rock towards the bear, and prepare to use your bear spray."

jewels.name: Waterproof layers, hat and gloves
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Bring high quality waterproof clothing: A reliably waterproof outer layer can keep you dry"; "Dress in layers: Start with a base layer to manage moisture... Wear an insulating layer such as a fleece jacket... Lastly, add a waterproof shell"; "Even during the relatively mild temperatures of summer, a warm hat and lightweight gloves can add significantly to your comfort level." On the trails: "Bring a rain jacket and rain pants on every hike."

jewels.name: Satellite communicator where there is no signal
jewels.blurb: NPS: "WiFi and cellular service are may be limited or nonesistant in most of the park" (sic), and Katmai "is a remote park that cannot be accessed by car. There are few services in the park and preserve."

jewels.name: Southwest Adventure Tours - 10-Day Ultimate Alaska Journey (TourRadar)
jewels.blurb: A 10-day guided trip from and to Anchorage, group size 4-10, ages 8+, with 2027 departures (June-August) listed; Day 3 of the itinerary: "Scenic flight to Katmai National Park and Preserve or Lake Clark National Park and Preserve" and a "Guided hike in Katmai or Lake Clark National Park" - Katmai is one of two named options, not a guarantee.

jewels.name: Katmai Junior Ranger
jewels.booking_route: none needed - free book at the visitor centers or online
jewels.blurb: "Junior Rangers are typically between the ages of 5 to 13, although people of all ages can participate. Get your free Junior Ranger book at the King Salmon and Brooks Camp visitor centers or download it here"; a ranger checks the book and swears you in, or you can mail it to the park and a patch is mailed back.

jewels.name: Cultural Walk and the Brooks River archaeology
jewels.blurb: "With over 900 house depressions near the river, this is one of the most densely concentrated archeological areas in North America." The ranger-led walk "follows an easy 1/4 mile trail to a reconstructed traditional Alutiiq/Sugpiaq home"; 2 p.m. daily June 7 to September 17 from the Brooks Camp Visitor Center, 45 minutes to 1 hour.

jewels.name: Brooks River bear cams (explore.org)
jewels.blurb: "Now you can follow the lives of the brown bears of Brooks River anywhere with an internet connection. Katmai National Park and explore.org have partnered to bring the bears to you." Rangers also host live chats on the cams: "Replays and recorded live chats can be found on explore.org's YouTube channel."

jewels.name: Fat Bear Week
jewels.blurb: "Fat Bear Week is an annual tournament celebrating their success in preparation for winter hibernation" - a single-elimination vote on the brown bears of Brooks River. "Matchups are open for voting September 22 - 29 between 12 - 9 p.m. Eastern / 9 a.m. - 6 p.m. Pacific / 8 a.m. - 5 p.m. Alaska."

jewels.name: Sea Hawk Air - floatplanes from Kodiak
jewels.booking_route: custom air charter by contact (rates not read)
jewels.blurb: Listed by the NPS among air taxis permitted in Katmai (Kodiak). In its own words: "Sea Hawk Air provides safe, reliable floatplane service across Kodiak Island and the Alaska Peninsula" for "fishing, viewing bears and wildlife, or embarking on your own wilderness adventure"; "Since 1987"; "Our de Havilland Beaver seats up to six passengers and carries up to 1,200 lbs of gear."

jewels.name: Katmai Wilderness Lodge
jewels.blurb: 🔴 CLOSED FOR 2026 by its own notice: "KWL is closed for 2026"; "we look forward to welcoming guests back when we reopen on June 1, 2027." Listed by the NPS among lodges in the park; it calls itself "the most remote bear lodge in Alaska" offering "a truly exclusive, small-group bear-viewin[g]" stay.

jewels.name: Crystal Creek Lodge
jewels.blurb: King Salmon fly-fishing and adventure lodge "Since 1988": "In our home waters of the Naknek River, anglers can reel in trout exceeding 30 inches in length"; it names "Katmai & Lake Clark National Park, Becharof & Alaska Peninsula National Wildlife Refuge, Aniakchak National Monument" as within reach.

jewels.name: King Salmon Lodge dining room and bar
jewels.booking_route: with a stay at King Salmon Lodge (kingsalmonlodge.com)
jewels.blurb: "Enjoy a drink at the cocktail bar, then indulge in a classically Alaskan meal of fresh-caught fish and locally grown produce in the riverside dining room, where large picture windows frame scenic views." (Natural Habitat Adventures' accommodation page for the lodge.)

jewels.name: King Salmon Visitor Center
jewels.booking_route: none needed - free; hours change seasonally
jewels.blurb: "Located just next door to the King Salmon Airport, the King Salmon Visitor Center is where you can find detailed information about the many federal public lands on the Alaska Peninsula as well as the Bristol Bay region." Exhibits, films and an Alaska Geographic bookstore; it also lends bear-resistant food containers and hands out the Junior Ranger book. The park headquarters is in King Salmon, "about 290 miles southwest of Anchorage" (NPS FAQ).

jewels.name: Evening Program, Brooks Camp Auditorium
jewels.blurb: "Join a park ranger for an illustrated talk in the Brooks Camp Auditorium. Each night, this program offers unique perspectives, stories, and information on Katmai National Park." 8 p.m. daily June 7 to September 17, 45 minutes to 1 hour.

jewels.name: Wilderness camping beyond Brooks Camp
jewels.booking_route: none needed - no fee or permit
jewels.blurb: "Wilderness camping is allowed everywhere in Katmai National Park outside of a 1.5-mile radius outside of Brooks Camp. There are no fees or permits required for wilderness camping." Via Dumpling Mountain (about 3 miles and 1,000 ft) or the Valley road (1.5 miles); "Camping in one location for more than 14 consecutive days is prohibited."

faq.q: How do you get to Katmai National Park?
faq.a: By air or boat. The NPS: "Most destinations are directly accessed via air taxi flights from Anchorage, Dillingham, Homer, King Salmon, Kodiak, and other nearby Alaska towns and villages. Regularly scheduled commercial flights to King Salmon (AKN) are available from Ted stevens Anchorage International Airport (ANC) via Alaska Airlines. Boats can access the Pacific coast of Katmai." Brooks Camp is reached by floatplane or by power boat from Naknek and King Salmon.

faq.q: Can you drive to Katmai National Park?
faq.a: No: "Unlike most parks in the United States, there are no roads connecting the park to the rest of the state -- you cannot drive to Katmai, Brooks Camp, or King Salmon from Anchorage. Most visitors fly or boat to the park."

faq.q: When is the best time to see bears in Katmai National Park?
faq.a: At Brooks Camp, July and September: "In July and September, bears are everywhere at Brooks Camp... During July, many bears can be seen fishing at Brooks Falls... In September, most bears are seen at the mouth of the Brooks River. Please note that in June and August few bears, if any, can be seen at Brooks Camp." On the coast at Hallo Bay, bears feed on sedges "Most commonly in June".

faq.q: Is there an entrance fee for Katmai National Park?
faq.a: No: "An entrance pass is not required to access Katmai National Park & Preserve." The Brooks Camp Campground ($18 per person per night in season) and a Brooks River Corridor permit ($6 Recreation.gov booking fee) carry their own fees.

faq.q: Can you camp in Katmai National Park?
faq.a: Yes, two ways: "Camping in a designated campground can only occur at Brooks Camp Campground" (reserved on Recreation.gov), and "Wilderness camping is allowed everywhere in Katmai National Park outside of a 1.5-mile radius outside of Brooks Camp. There are no fees or permits required for wilderness camping." Bear-resistant food containers are mandatory in all backcountry areas.

faq.q: Where can you stay in Katmai National Park?
faq.a: At Brooks Camp: "You can stay at Brooks Lodge or camp in the Brooks Camp Campground. For information on rates and reservations for Brooks Lodge, visit Katmailand.com... Campground reservations can be made on recreation.gov." Brooks Lodge rooms are allocated by Katmailand's lottery.

faq.q: What is the weather like in Katmai National Park?
faq.a: "On average, wet and cool conditions predominate in spring, summer, and fall. Summer temperatures range from 30˚ to 80˚ Fahrenheit (-1˚ to 27˚ Celsius). Winters are drier and colder." "Strong winds are common all year." The NPS advises waterproof clothing, layers, and a warm hat and lightweight gloves even in summer.

faq.q: Can you fish in Katmai National Park?
faq.a: Yes. "An Alaska sport fishing license is required of all nonresidents 16 and over and most residents 16 to 59." "Special federal regulations, in addition to state regulations, exist for the Brooks River." Near bears, "Fishing must be terminated within 50 yards of any bear".

faq.q: Where can you watch the Katmai bear cam?
faq.a: Online, through explore.org: "Now you can follow the lives of the brown bears of Brooks River anywhere with an internet connection. Katmai National Park and explore.org have partnered to bring the bears to you."

faq.q: When is Fat Bear Week at Katmai National Park?
faq.a: "Fat Bear Week is an annual tournament celebrating their success in preparation for winter hibernation." "Matchups are open for voting September 22 - 29 between 12 - 9 p.m. Eastern / 9 a.m. - 6 p.m. Pacific / 8 a.m. - 5 p.m. Alaska."

seo.meta_title: Katmai National Park: Brooks Falls Bears & How to Get There | TravelWell
seo.meta_description: No roads, free entry: fly in to Brooks Falls bears in July and September, the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes, Brooks Lodge by lottery and the NPS campground.

name: Lake Clark National Park
line: Coastal brown bears, volcanoes and Proenneke's cabin

jewels.name: Chinitna Bay bear viewing
jewels.booking_route: none needed in the park - no entrance pass; reached by air taxi or a guided bear-viewing operator
jewels.blurb: "Located at the southern end the park's Cook Inlet coast, Chinitna Bay offers world class bear viewing. Visitors may be able to see as many as twenty coastal brown bears from a single location." "Most visitors arrive in a small plane operating on wheels that lands on the beach" - under an hour from Homer, Kenai or Anchorage - or by boat from Homer Harbor, "four to five hours". Three designated viewing sites with marked trails; the sedge meadow beyond the river is closed due to high bear use.

jewels.name: Silver Salmon Creek
jewels.booking_route: none needed in the park; reached by wheeled plane on the beach or a lodge transfer
jewels.blurb: "Located midway up the park's Cook Inlet coast, this is the place to be if you are interested in bear viewing or fishing." Bears graze the sedge meadows late spring to mid-summer and fish in late summer; "Coho (silver) salmon and humpback (pink) salmon as well as Dolly Varden run up the creek in the late summer." Ranger station on the south side of the creek; the sedge meadow "is closed to human entry between the Sargent Creek confluence and the Silver Salmon Creek from June 15 to September 15 for habitat restoration."

jewels.name: Crescent Lake
jewels.booking_route: none needed in the park; reached by floatplane
jewels.blurb: "Crescent Lake is tucked into the coastal Chigmit Mountains, with views of Redoubt Volcano, high bear populations, and strong salmon runs" - "the park's most visited destination." "Sockeye / red salmon arrive during the month of July, while coho/silver salmon come in mid August through early September." "Camping is not recommended at Crescent Lake due to the high number of bears in the area".

jewels.name: Proenneke Cabin, Upper Twin Lake
jewels.booking_route: none needed - a free historic site; reached by floatplane
jewels.blurb: "Richard Proenneke's home on Upper Twin Lake is a popular destination for visitors to the park", on the lake's south shore "immediately up-lake of the Hope Creek delta." "Open: Late May (tentative) through late September", 10:00 AM to 4:00 PM for 2026, with rangers and volunteers housed nearby. "Visitors arrive by small planes that land on Upper Twin Lake" - just over an hour from Anchorage, typically 30 minutes from Port Alsworth. "Camping is prohibited within the National Historic Register boundaries".

jewels.name: Tanalian Falls Trail
jewels.booking_route: none needed - free park trail from Port Alsworth
jewels.blurb: "Length: about 4 miles round trip": "Meander through birch groves and up spruce studded hillsides to a stunning view of Lake Clark", to a 30-foot waterfall over ancient lava. The Tanalian trails network "begins in town" at Port Alsworth.

jewels.name: Port Alsworth Visitor Center
jewels.booking_route: none needed - free; 1 Park Place, Port Alsworth, AK 99653; 907-644-3626
jewels.blurb: "The visitor center is located midway up the easternmost runway" at the park's field headquarters, "Open in the summer only." "The visitor center has a wheelchair accessible ramp. A fat tire wheelchair that works well on gravel is available from the Park HQ". Port Alsworth "offers visitor services such as lodging, air taxis, guide services, gear rentals, post office, and park visitor center."

jewels.name: Lake Clark Junior Ranger programme
jewels.booking_route: none needed - free, in person or by mail
jewels.blurb: "Pick up your free Junior Ranger Activity Book at the Visitor Center in Port Alsworth, or speak with a backcountry ranger"; or "Download a PDF of Junior Ranger Journey and Where There Are Bears to print out on your own or email us to request a copy of the Activity Book and Badge to be mailed to you." A ranger signs the book, leads the pledge and presents "an official badge."

jewels.name: Kontrashibuna Lake Trail
jewels.blurb: "Length: about 5.5 miles round trip": "Beyond Tanalian Falls, the trail enters Lake Clark's designated wilderness on its way to the serenity of Kontrashibuna Lake, a spectacular mountain gem." "Intrepid hikers with more time can extend a trip beyond Kontrashibuna Lake into the trailless high country."

jewels.name: Tanalian Mountain Trail
jewels.blurb: "Length: 8.6 miles round trip": "The trail up Tanalian Mountain is steep and rigorous with stunning panoramic views of Lake Clark and the surrounding mountains"; it needs at least eight hours.

jewels.name: Beaver Pond Trail
jewels.blurb: "Length: 3.2 miles round trip": "This trail meanders through quiet birch groves and past an old beaver pond where shorebirds nest in the early summer."

jewels.name: Priest Rock Public Use Cabin
jewels.blurb: On Lake Clark's north shore about 8 miles from Port Alsworth: "Stay in a rustic cabin to experience remote Alaska living for yourself." Sleeps up to six (three single beds and one queen); "$65 per night"; maximum "5 nights for a limit of 21 nights in a calendar year." "Cabin is only accessible by floatplane or boat; water taxis may be available from Port Alsworth."

jewels.name: Hope Creek campsite, Upper Twin Lake
jewels.blurb: "Primitive camping area with no services" on Upper Twin Lake with bear-resistant boxes provided; a creek crossing leads to the Proenneke cabin. "Camping at Hope Creek Campsite is limited to a total of 14 days," with first-come, first-served hardened tent sites.

jewels.name: Wild river rafting: Mulchatna, Chilikadrotna, Tlikakila
jewels.booking_route: none needed - self-supported, by air-taxi drop-off
jewels.blurb: The NPS names the "Mulchatna, Chilikadrotna, Tlikakila" rivers for rafting, and notes that visitors do not need fees or permits for river running. "With 187 species documented in the park, Lake Clark is a fantastic place to visit for birding."

jewels.name: Nat Hab's Alaska Bear Camp, Chinitna Bay
jewels.booking_route: sold only inside Natural Habitat Adventures trips; 800-543-8917
jewels.blurb: Natural Habitat Adventures' camp at Chinitna Bay, Lake Clark National Park: ten handcrafted cabins with twin beds, en suite bathroom, hot running water and propane heat; "Located on the ancestral lands of the Dena'ina people, Alaska Bear Camp is designed to tread lightly" - on a historic homestead, the only privately held inholding grandfathered within the park since 1980. Guests arrive by chartered bush plane from Homer, landing on the beach in front of camp. The NPS lists it among Chinitna Bay lodging, (800) 543-8917.

jewels.name: Alaska Bear Camp Photo Expedition (Natural Habitat Adventures)
jewels.blurb: A 7-day multi-day guided trip "Limited to 14 travelers": it begins with a chartered bush plane flight from Homer across Cook Inlet to the camp on a 15-acre inholding within Lake Clark National Park; bears watched from a two-story viewing platform, on foot with naturalist guides and from the Bear Mobile. Departure month July; "From $10695 (+air)".

jewels.name: Silver Salmon Creek Lodge
jewels.blurb: "Silver Salmon Creek Lodge is a premier vacation destination for wildlife photography, world-class sport fishing and Alaska bear viewing", "along the western shores of Cook Inlet"; "a one hour flight by small plane from Anchorage". "Bear viewing services are offered from June through mid-September"; "1-7 day excursions" with "a choice of a fully catered trip or remote tent camping." (907) 690-1299.

jewels.name: Redoubt Mountain Lodge, Crescent Lake
jewels.blurb: "Redoubt Mountain Lodge is exclusively located on the glacier-fed waters of Crescent Lake in the heart of Lake Clark National Park, Alaska", about 8 miles from 10,197-foot Redoubt Volcano. "Accessible only by floatplane or helicopter and being the only lodge or privately owned property in the area"; bear viewing, fishing, hiking, kayaking and helicopter fly-outs.

jewels.name: Lake Clark Resort (The Farm Lodge), Port Alsworth
jewels.blurb: Operates "The Farm Lodge" on the southwest shore of Lake Clark, within walking distance of park headquarters and trailheads; onsite cabins plus "Wilderness Cabins" about a 10-minute walk away; all-inclusive packages with bear viewing, fishing, flightseeing, rafting and Proenneke cabin trips; June through September; run by the Alsworth family since 1977.

jewels.name: Ultimate Alaska Adventure package (Lake Clark Resort)
jewels.blurb: A 9-day package from Port Alsworth: lodging with private bath, "home-cooked Alaskan meals", scenic bush plane tours (Lake Clark Pass, Katmai, Alaska Peninsula), "Guided bear viewing" at Brooks Camp in Katmai, mountain-lake tours, a boat tour on Lake Clark and local hiking. The price shown on the page was not a usable figure and is not stated here.

jewels.name: Rust's Flying Service - Lake Clark National Park Bear Viewing
jewels.blurb: From Lake Hood, Anchorage ("Lake Hood's oldest and largest seaplane operator"): "Enjoy an hour and ten-minute stunning flightseeing tour via floatplane from Anchorage to Lake Clark National Park and Preserve"; bears viewed at Crescent Lake "by covered pontoon boat to lakeside areas where bears feed on spawning wild Alaska salmon". "11 hours Departs 9am", "August 1 - September 25"; $1,445 per person plus 3% transportation tax and $15 NPS fee.

jewels.name: Smokey Bay Air, Homer
jewels.blurb: "Fly from scenic Homer, Alaska across the Cook Inlet to either Katmai National Park or Lake Clark National Park to view brown bears"; it calls Lake Clark "home to the highest concentrations of Alaskan Grizzly/Coastal Brown Bears". Listed by the NPS as a Homer air taxi. 907-531-0602.

jewels.name: Alaska West Air, Kenai
jewels.blurb: "Delivering unforgettable Alaska tours in Kenai, AK, since 1978" from "the heart of the Kenai Peninsula": bear viewing, fly-out fishing, hunting, flightseeing and custom charters on a fleet of nine aircraft. Listed by the NPS as a Kenai/Soldotna air taxi for Lake Clark. (907) 283-4292.

jewels.name: Lake Clark Air
jewels.blurb: "Service You Can Count On Since 1977" - founded by bush pilot Glen Alsworth Sr.; seat fares, charters and freight with offices in Port Alsworth (907-781-2211) and at Merrill Field, Anchorage (907-278-2054). The NPS lists it for flights from both Anchorage and Port Alsworth.

jewels.name: Tulch'ina Adventures campground and cabins, Port Alsworth
jewels.blurb: "Cabin rentals and campground in Port Alsworth, AK" - the Tanalian Cabin and Dry Creek Cabins - plus "Water taxi, charter boat and freight services on Lake Clark". The NPS names it as Port Alsworth's one privately operated campground. 1 Tanalian Point; (907) 782-4720.

jewels.name: Tulch'ina Adventures kayak and gear rentals
jewels.blurb: "Kayak and gear rentals for Lake Clark National Park" from Port Alsworth, alongside its water taxi to the lake's cabins and trailheads. No rates are published on the page.

jewels.name: Homer Spit Campground
jewels.blurb: "WHERE THE LAND ENDS AND THE SEA BEGINS": "large, full hookup sites for motorhomes up to 40'" and "Small tent spaces for the lone backpacker"; "2026 season May 6th - September 9th", online reservations opening January 1, 2026; 4535 Homer Spit Road - the spit is where the Homer bear-viewing flights and boats depart.

jewels.name: Kilcher Homestead MiracleMeadow, Homer
jewels.blurb: On the Kilcher Homestead, hosted by Stellavera Kilcher: glamping in the "Awesome Glamping Island Tent" (canvas, sleeps 4), the "Kilcher Homestead Lighthouse" cabin with heater and a cedar cabin, plus a $45/night tent site; "full outdoor kitchen", views of glaciers and Kachemak Bay; Homer is "35 minutes away".

jewels.name: Seaside Farm, Kachemak Bay
jewels.blurb: A 30-acre farm on Kachemak Bay near Homer, listed by Hipcamp under Cabins & Glamping: three cabins (Seashell, Beach Hideaway, Wildflower), 10 tent sites and 4 van sites; covered camping pavilion with outdoor kitchen, "trails, lawns, gardens, trees, hay fields, and a private beach".

jewels.name: The Saltry, Halibut Cove
jewels.blurb: Listed by the Homer Chamber of Commerce under the bay: "The Saltry Halibut Cove SUN-SAT Fine Dining | 907-226-2424" (Dining Guide, "Updated July 8, 2026").

jewels.name: Land's End Chart Room
jewels.blurb: Homer Chamber of Commerce Dining Guide: "Land's End Chart Room 4786 Homer Spit Rd. SUN-SAT Seaside Fine Dining | 907-235-0406".

jewels.name: Captain Pattie's Fish House
jewels.blurb: Homer Chamber of Commerce Dining Guide: "Captain Pattie's Fish House 4241 Homer Spit Rd. SUN-SAT Seafood | 907-235-5135".

jewels.name: La Baleine Cafe
jewels.blurb: Homer Chamber of Commerce Dining Guide: "La Baleine Cafe 4460 Homer Spit Rd. WED-SUN Locally Sourced Cafe |907-299-6672".

jewels.name: Harbor Grill
jewels.blurb: Homer Chamber of Commerce Dining Guide: "Harbor Grill 4264 Homer Spit Rd. SUN-SAT Seafood & Steak | 907-235-9333".

jewels.name: Fat Olives Restaurant
jewels.booking_route: walk-in (no booking method in the guide)
jewels.blurb: Homer Chamber of Commerce Dining Guide: "Fat Olives Restaurant 276 Ohlson Ln. SUN-SAT Pizza, seafood, pasta, sandwiches".

jewels.name: Homer Brewing Company
jewels.blurb: Homer Chamber of Commerce Dining Guide: "Homer Brewing Company 1411 Lakeshore Dr. SUN-SAT Traditional Brewery | 907-235-3626".

jewels.name: AJ's OldTown Steakhouse
jewels.blurb: Homer Chamber of Commerce Dining Guide: "AJ's OldTown Steakhouse 120 W. Bunnell Ave. TUE-SAT Steaks & Seafood | 907-235-9949".

jewels.name: Bear-resistant food container for every camp
jewels.booking_route: free loan at the Port Alsworth visitor center; to own one, affiliate referral to BearVault (AvantLink)
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Proper Food Storage is Required"; "A bear resistant food container must hold all scented items, including toothpaste and sunscreen - not just food." The park "offers bear resistant containers for temporary use by visitors free of charge at the park visitor center in Port Alsworth." At Crescent Lake caught fish must be "secured in an approved bear-resistant container as soon as you catch it."

jewels.name: Bear spray, carried ready
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Unholster your bear spray and be prepared to use it if necessary"; "Use pepper spray if the bear comes within range if you have it." In an encounter: "Remain calm and do not run." "If it is a brown bear, play dead." "If it is a black bear, fight back vigorously!"

jewels.name: Rain gear, waterproof footwear and layers
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Sturdy rain gear and waterproof footwear are a must, and smart travelers make sure to layer clothing." "The coast is often foggy and wet, with an average annual rainfall of 40 to 80 inches"; on the Tanalian trails, "make sure you are prepared to spend the night if unexpected weather makes that necessary."

faq.q: How do you get to Lake Clark National Park?
faq.a: By small plane. The NPS: "Like many areas in Alaska, Lake Clark is not on the road system and travel takes place primarily by small plane." The park is "65 air miles northwest of Homer, and about 120 air miles southwest of Anchorage", and the NPS lists air taxis from Anchorage, Homer, Kenai or Soldotna, King Salmon, Kodiak, Port Alsworth and Wasilla.

faq.q: Can you drive to Lake Clark National Park?
faq.a: No. "Lake Clark is not on the road system; therefore, access is primarily by small aircraft."

faq.q: Can you get to Lake Clark National Park by boat?
faq.a: On the coast, sometimes: "When weather and tides permit, the east side of the park on the Cook Inlet coast may be accessed by boat via an open-ocean crossing." To Chinitna Bay, boat travel from Homer Harbor takes "four to five hours" over "approximately 60 miles".

faq.q: What is the best time to see bears in Lake Clark National Park?
faq.a: The NPS describes two seasons on the coast: late spring through mid-summer, when bears graze the sedge meadows, and late summer, when they gather at the rivers for the salmon - "Coho (silver) salmon and humpback (pink) salmon as well as Dolly Varden run up the creek in the late summer" at Silver Salmon Creek.

faq.q: How big is Lake Clark National Park?
faq.a: "Comprised of 4 million acres on the Alaska Peninsula in southwest Alaska."

faq.q: When was Lake Clark National Park established?
faq.a: "Established by the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act (ANILCA) on December 2, 1980."

faq.q: Can you camp at Lake Clark National Park?
faq.a: Yes. Backcountry camping is generally permitted with bear-resistant canisters required; Hope Creek on Upper Twin Lake is a "Primitive camping area with no services" with bear-resistant boxes; Port Alsworth has one privately operated campground. Camping is prohibited at the Proenneke Historic Site, and the Chinitna Bay sedge meadow is closed to camping May 1-August 31.

faq.q: Does Lake Clark National Park have a visitor center?
faq.a: Yes, in Port Alsworth: "The visitor center is located midway up the easternmost runway", "Open in the summer only." Winter visitors may contact staff at the headquarters building next door.

faq.q: Do you need tickets for Lake Clark National Park and Preserve?
faq.a: No: "An entrance pass is not required to access Lake Clark National Park & Preserve." The public use cabins carry fees and "Reservations are required."

faq.q: Can you fish in Lake Clark National Park?
faq.a: Yes. At Crescent Lake "Sockeye / red salmon arrive during the month of July, while coho/silver salmon come in mid August through early September", and any fish caught must be "secured in an approved bear-resistant container as soon as you catch it."

seo.meta_title: Lake Clark National Park: Bears, Proenneke Cabin & Fly-In Lodges | TravelWell
