name: Gates of the Arctic National Park
line: Roadless Brooks Range wilderness and rivers

jewels.name: Trail-less Brooks Range backpacking
jewels.booking_route: none needed - no entrance pass or registration; reached by air taxi or on foot from the Dalton Highway or Anaktuvuk Pass
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Backpackers have 8.4 million acres of spectacular wilderness in which they can wander at will." There are no designated trails; "Topographic maps are essential in planning your course of travel", and "Group size limit is 10 people, to minimize impacts to the environment." The NPS names Boreal Mountain and Frigid Crags above the Koyukuk River.

jewels.name: Six Wild Rivers float trips
jewels.booking_route: none needed in the park; self-outfitted or with a guided rafting operator, dropped by air taxi
jewels.blurb: The park holds six designated Wild Rivers - the Alatna, John, Kobuk, Noatak, North Fork Koyukuk (which "flows south through the 'Gates of the Arctic'") and Tinayguk. "Waters average Class I and II, with a few Class II-IV rapids"; "the highest water is in May and June." The NPS weather page: "July through August is generally the best time to take float trips."

jewels.name: Anaktuvuk Pass Nunamiut village
jewels.booking_route: none needed - scheduled flight from Fairbanks; designated camping by the airstrip
jewels.blurb: "Situated inside the park's boundaries, at the top of a wide 2,100 foot mountain pass, the village of Anaktuvuk Pass is a great place to start your exploration of Gates of the Arctic." "Accessible by commercial air service from Fairbanks." The city council designated camping "around the access road on the east side of the airstrip"; private lands: "There is no allowed permission to travel across or camp on these parcels of private property." Ranger station "Staffed each year between April to the end of September."

jewels.name: Simon Paneak Memorial Museum
jewels.blurb: In Anaktuvuk Pass: "Exhibits on Nunamiut history, life, and culture", admission listed by the NPS at $20, phone 907-661-3413. The NPS history page: "In the late 1940s bands of nomadic Nunamiut Eskimos settled in Anaktuvuk Pass. Today their village represents a combination of modern and traditional lifeways."

jewels.name: Bettles Ranger Station and visitor center
jewels.booking_route: none needed - free; open 7 days a week July 1 to September 25 (accessibility page)
jewels.blurb: "Bettles hosts a park visitor center, where travelers attend backcountry orientations, receive park condition updates, attend ranger programs, stamp their national park passport, and check out bear resistant food containers." Bettles Field sits "around 20 miles south of the southern boundaries" of the park, reached by "scheduled commercial air service from Fairbanks." The accessibility page: entrance "via an ADA accessible ramp. Accessible restrooms are available."

jewels.name: Gravel-bar and lakeshore camping
jewels.booking_route: none needed - dispersed backcountry camping, no reservations
jewels.blurb: "There are no designated campsites in Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve." "Gravel bars make excellent campsites since they often have fewer mosquitoes than other sites, and high water will erase signs of your presence" - but "locate your camp well above current water levels." The NPS suggests "moving camp every 2-3 days" and keeping "tent, cook, and BRFC are all 100 yards apart in a triangle formation."

jewels.name: Agiak Lake hunting blinds and inuksuit
jewels.booking_route: none needed - backcountry, reached by air taxi
jewels.blurb: An NPS place page: Agiak Lake has "stone hunting blinds and hundreds of rock cairns (inuksuit)" used in caribou hunting practiced for thousands of years. "People have lived in the Brooks Range for more than 13,000 years and thousands of archeological sites in Gates of the Arctic document this history." Leave all "cultural, and historical resources where you found them" (camping page).

jewels.name: Preserve sport hunting under state licence
jewels.booking_route: State of Alaska licence via the Alaska Department of Fish and Game; guided hunts through an NPS-authorized guide
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Sport hunting and trapping are permitted in Gates of the Arctic National Preserve, but not in Gates of the Arctic National Park." An Alaska State hunting licence is required for hunters 16 or older, under State regulations for Game Management Units 23, 24 and 26; guided hunts need an NPS Concession Contract or Commercial Use Authorization.

jewels.name: Caribou, bears, Dall sheep and muskox
jewels.booking_route: none needed - seen in the backcountry or from a flightseeing aircraft
jewels.blurb: NPS wildlife page: "Caribou trek from their boreal forest wintering grounds to their calving areas on the coastal plain"; "Grizzly and black bears leave their dens with cubs born the previous winter"; Dall's sheep, muskox, lynx, beavers and snowshoe hares each carry their own section, and "Whitefish, northern pike and grayling feast in the rivers and lakes."

jewels.name: Winter aurora and ski or dog travel
jewels.booking_route: none needed in the park; aurora and mushing trips are sold by the gateway lodges
jewels.blurb: NPS: "November through March is the best time for viewing the Aurora Borealis." "February through April is a good time for winter travel with skis, snowshoes, or dogs", with "ice crossings, potential avalanche conditions and extreme temperatures (-50F or colder)."

jewels.name: Flightseeing, fishing and fly-in camp-outs
jewels.booking_route: through an air taxi in Bettles, Coldfoot or Fairbanks
jewels.blurb: NPS things to do: "Local air taxis provide flight-seeing trips, day trips or overnight camp-outs at remote locations." "Spend the day fishing at an alpine lake, watching the caribou pass through northern valleys." "Lakes and gravel bars provide camping spots surrounded by unparalleled natural beauty."

jewels.name: Gates of the Arctic Base Camp (Arctic Wild)
jewels.booking_route: reservation request form at arcticwild.com/reservation-form/, deposit required; info@arcticwild.com, 907.479.8203
jewels.blurb: A multi-day guided base camp in the central Brooks Range, August 9-13, 2027, $8,200: pre-trip meeting in Fairbanks, charter flight to a tundra base camp, three days of day hikes to "glacial cirques, alpine lakes, ridges", return to Fairbanks. "You need not be a seasoned adventurer to enjoy this trip." Included: "Transportation beyond Fairbanks, Food while in the wilderness, Stoves, cooking & eating utensils, Safety & repair gear, Professional guide service." Arctic Wild's 2027 Gates list also carries a 4-day Gates and Kobuk Valley base camp ($9,100), a 10-day Noatak River canoe ($9,600) and an 11-day Arrigetch Peaks packraft ($9,900).

jewels.name: Arrigetch-Alatna Pack Raft (Alaska Alpine Adventures)
jewels.blurb: A guided "Arrigetch-Alatna Pack Raft - Gates of the Arctic National Park": 12 days, backpacking, multisport and rafting, "35+ miles, 50+ river miles", intensity Level 3, $8,195. The same operator lists the 10-day "Oolah Valley High Route" ($6,695) and a 12-day Noatak River and Great Kobuk Sand Dunes combination across Gates of the Arctic and Kobuk Valley ($9,695).

jewels.name: Bettles Lodge, the 1950 gateway lodge
jewels.booking_route: email info@bettleslodge.com or 1-907-692-5111; "50% deposit" at booking (FAQ)
jewels.blurb: "Bettles is located 35 miles north of the Arctic Circle", the "jumping off" point for Gates of the Arctic, Noatak and Kobuk Valley; "Serving the Arctic Traveler since 1950." The historic lodge was "Completed in 1950" and "became recognized as a National Historic Site in the year 1996": "6 cozy rooms", plus the Aurora Lodge's "4 Jacuzzi rooms". Winter brings Northern Lights viewing, dog mushing and cross-country skiing. FAQ: "Nope" to wheelchair access - guests "climb 4 stairs into the Cessna".

jewels.name: National Park Collector fly-in day (Bettles Lodge)
jewels.blurb: "Our same day 'National Park Collector Wilderness Adventure' can take you to both the Gates of Arctic and Kobuk National Park in the same day" by float plane (Cessna 180 or DeHavilland Beaver), with a picnic lunch and landings in the parks. "We require at least two nights in Bettles to join on our National Park Adventure." No price on the page: "Please contact us for price quotes and questions."

jewels.name: Brooks Range Aviation, Bettles air taxi
jewels.blurb: Based at Bettles Field, flying "Gates of Arctic National Park, Naotak National Preserve, Kobuk Valley National Park" and the refuges. Its "most popular tour", Gates of the Arctic and Kobuk Valley, "typically lasts 4 to 5 hours" with landings, minimum two passengers, $1,995 per person for two down to $1,595 for six. Gates routes land at an Arrigetch Peaks lake or fly the North Fork Koyukuk "through 'The Gates'"; unguided float-plane drop-offs for the Noatak, John, Alatna and Killik rivers.

jewels.name: Iniakuk Lake Wilderness Lodge
jewels.blurb: "Iniakuk Lake Wilderness Lodge is an exclusive fly-in luxury wilderness lodge 220 miles (350 km) north of Fairbanks in Alaska's Brooks Range", on the edge of Gates of the Arctic, family-owned since 1974 and built by hand from local logs. Winter February 20 - April 10, summer June 20 - September 10; "all-inclusive fly-out tours begin and end in Fairbanks". Northern lights, dog mushing, float trips, hiking, canoeing, fishing.

jewels.name: Arctic Interagency Visitor Center, Coldfoot
jewels.booking_route: none needed - free; group programmes arranged in advance
jewels.blurb: At "Milepost 175" of the Dalton Highway: exhibits and films on the Arctic, an "evening program", "Educational programs for groups" by advance arrangement, trip planning, bear barrel loans and "Backcountry registration for Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve." "Open 12 p.m. - 9 p.m., late May through mid-September, including holidays." Entry is free.

jewels.name: Slate Creek Inn at Coldfoot Camp
jewels.booking_route: online via the Mews booking engine linked from coldfootcamp.com; (907) 474-3500
jewels.blurb: Coldfoot Camp, "Mile 175 Dalton Hwy": "Each cozy, clean room has two twin beds and a private bathroom with a shower", in refurbished trailers that once housed pipeline construction workers. "$259 per night single or double occupancy" through Dec 1, 2025; $269 from January 1, 2026. Fully refundable until 7 days before arrival. Open year-round.

jewels.name: Coldfoot Camp tent sites and RV hook-ups
jewels.booking_route: at the Coldfoot Camp front desk, (907) 474-3500
jewels.blurb: Coldfoot Camp's own page: "Camping is available at Coldfoot Camp during the summer months, free of charge", with 24-hour cafe bathrooms and water; showers $14 at the front desk. Alaska.org adds: "Limited RV hook-ups area available for a fee" and "Open May through September, weather permitting" (alaska.org is a guide site; the camp's own stay page does not mention hook-ups).

jewels.name: Marion Creek Campground (BLM)
jewels.booking_route: first-come, first-served; pay on site via the Recreation.gov app
jewels.blurb: At "mile 180 of the Dalton Highway", 5 miles north of Coldfoot: 27 campsites, "Fourteen sites are pull-through", "$12 per night", "mid-May through end of September (depending on snowfall)", "first-come, first-serve basis only" with payment by QR code through the Recreation.gov app. Potable water, vault toilets, fire rings, a camp host; no electricity or dump station.

jewels.name: Wiseman Village Visit from Coldfoot
jewels.blurb: "Drive thirteen miles North on the Dalton Highway and 'travel back in time' to visit the historic gold mining village" - $69 per person, year-round, booked at 907-474-3500. The NPS: Coldfoot and Wiseman sit "along the Middle Fork of the Koyukuk River", "north of the Arctic Circle", and "Some lodging is available in the town" of Wiseman. Winter adds the "Arctic Village Aurora" trip to Wiseman, August 21 to April 21, $89.

jewels.name: Gates of the Arctic Air Adventure from Coldfoot
jewels.blurb: Coldfoot Camp: "Sightsee in some of the most remote parts of the Arctic via bush plane" - a 1-hour flight, June through August, $329 per person. Also from the camp: "Float down the Koyukuk River with an experienced raft guide!" (mid-May to mid-September, $149) and the Arctic Mountain Safari "past timberline to the Arctic tundra" ($129).

jewels.name: Arctic Circle Midnight Sun Overnight Adventure (Northern Alaska Tour Company)
jewels.booking_route: Northern Alaska Tour Company planning page; 800-474-1986
jewels.blurb: "An Overnight Guided Round Trip Journey By Land And Air Into Alaska's Brooks Mountain Range" from Fairbanks: the Dalton Highway, the Arctic Circle Trading Post in Joy, the Yukon River, an overnight at Coldfoot Camp with optional Gates of the Arctic air flights, Wiseman visits and Koyukuk River floats. 3 days / 2 nights per the page; "$639 *Per person based on double occupancy" (April-June) and "$739" (June-August), 2027 season April 22 - August 20. The company: "Northern Alaska Tour Company pioneered Arctic Circle touring on Alaska's Dalton Highway."

jewels.name: Gates of the Arctic Air Adventure from Fairbanks
jewels.booking_route: Northern Alaska Tour Company planning page; 800-474-1986
jewels.blurb: Northern Alaska Tour Company: "An Evening Round Trip Journey By Air In To The Gates Of The Arctic National Park" - departs Fairbanks 7:00 PM, lands at Coldfoot "60 miles north of the Arctic Circle", flies through the park, back in Fairbanks between 11:30 PM and midnight. Daily "June 1, 2027 - August 31, 2027"; $749 per person (2026 rate), $769 (2027).

jewels.name: Arctic Getaway Cabin and Breakfast, Wiseman
jewels.blurb: "Located along the Dalton Highway north of Coldfoot, our cozy cabins are tucked away in Wiseman in the scenic foothills of the Brooks range." Three cabins with private bathrooms and kitchens, breakfast included, open year-round; nightly rates listed at $210 to $350.

jewels.name: Wright Air Service scheduled flights
jewels.blurb: "Proudly Serving Alaska Since 1966", from Fairbanks with daily scheduled service to over 40 interior and northern villages including Bettles, Anaktuvuk Pass and Coldfoot; charters to "most locations in Alaska, including National Parks", and flightseeing. Bettles Lodge's FAQ: its guests fly Fairbanks-Bettles on Wright Air Service.

jewels.name: Coldfoot Trucker's Cafe buffets
jewels.blurb: "The Coldfoot Trucker's Cafe is open year-round, but our offerings change seasonally." Summer: "a full breakfast buffet from 5 am - 9 am, and a dinner buffet from 5 pm - 9 pm" - breakfast $16.95, dinner $27.95, with discounts for children 12 and under; sack lunches to order. Winter: menu "all day, from 5am to 12am."

jewels.name: Frozen Foot Saloon, Coldfoot
jewels.blurb: "The Frozen Foot Saloon offers a variety of beer and wine for your enjoyment" - Silver Gulch beers brewed in Fairbanks, Alaskan Amber and Matanuska, wines from Merlot to Moscato. "We do not serve liquor at this time." Mile 175, Dalton Highway.

jewels.name: Bettles Lodge dining room and bar
jewels.booking_route: walk-in in summer; included in lodge packages
jewels.blurb: Summer: "Full service dining room & bar in the Lodge lobby" (accommodations page). Package guests: "All meals, snacks, soft-drinks are included in your package price" - "hand cut steak or prime rib, Sockeye Salmon, chicken" with "Chef's choice of starch, veg and dessert" (FAQ, https://bettleslodge.com/faqs/).

jewels.name: Alaska Commercial store, Anaktuvuk Pass
jewels.blurb: The NPS lists the village's Alaska Commercial store, open "Monday-Saturday 10-6. Closed Sundays.", phone 907-661-3327 - the one place inside the park boundary to resupply food. The NPS basic info page: carry extra food provisions for weather delays that ground aircraft.

jewels.name: Bettles Lodge camping supplies and cold-weather kit
jewels.blurb: The lodge sells "Camping supplies (bear spray, fuel, propane)" and has a gift shop (park collector page). Winter guests are kitted out: "parkas, snow pants, heavy bunny boots or Sorel brand boots, gloves, mitts, ski goggles", and rubber boots for float-plane access (FAQ). Summer advice: "Always, always, bring your own rain gear" and "Have layers with you just in case."

jewels.name: Arctic Wild raft and camping gear rentals
jewels.blurb: Fairbanks-based Arctic Wild - "Professionally guided Alaska adventure tours in Alaska's vast wilderness" - offers raft rentals (site navigation), and its Gates base camp page states camping gear is available for rental against the personal equipment list; personal clothing and fishing equipment are not included.

jewels.name: Bear-resistant food container for every camp
jewels.booking_route: free loan at Bettles, Coldfoot, Anaktuvuk Pass or Fairbanks; to own one, affiliate referral to BearVault (AvantLink)
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Proper food storage (certified bear resistant food container) is required in all Alaskan parks" (camping page). "Gates of the Arctic ranger stations and visitor centers have a variety of BRFCs available for loan, free of charge, on a first come, first served basis"; they can be returned to any ranger station or by mail. Coolers, plastic totes, dry bags and kayaks are not approved.

jewels.name: Bear spray, carried ready
jewels.booking_route: affiliate referral to Counter Assault (AvantLink); sold at Bettles Lodge
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Bear spray (Capsicum spray) is also an effective deterrent in bear encounters", effective at 15-20 feet; do not spray downwind. The park holds grizzly and black bears: for brown bear contact, play dead; for black bears, fight back - never play dead.

jewels.name: Maps, compass, GPS and a satellite communicator
jewels.booking_route: affiliate referral to rei.com (AvantLink); Garmin inReach has no published programme
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Topographic maps are essential in planning your course of travel"; "Carry your maps and a good compass (and a GPS unit is strongly encouraged if you have access to one)" (backpacking page). Basic info: there is no cellular service; bring two forms of communication - "Satellite phones are an excellent method of two-way communication in Alaska's backcountry", and messaging devices with emergency SOS are available for rental in Fairbanks.

jewels.name: Insect protection, rain gear and layers
jewels.booking_route: affiliate referral to rei.com (AvantLink) or Amazon Associates
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Insect protection is a must during the summer months"; thunderstorms are frequent June through July, so bring rain gear and layered clothing - snow can fall in nearly every month, so "always be prepared for colder-than-expected conditions." Self-contained stoves are "strongly recommended. Fires are often impractical" (camping page).

faq.q: How do I get to Gates of the Arctic National Park?
faq.a: Through Fairbanks, then by air or on foot. The NPS: "Access to the park begins in Fairbanks, Alaska" and "Most visitors access the park by air taxi, in small aircraft equipped with floats or tundra tires." Gateways are Bettles (a visitor center, and "Visitors can fly into the park from Bettles"), Anaktuvuk Pass ("Fly into this small Nunamuit village on one of the daily flights from Fairbanks and walk into the park from the airstrip") and Coldfoot ("Drive 280 miles north from Fairbanks up the Dalton Highway or fly in").

faq.q: Can you drive to Gates of the Arctic National Park?
faq.a: Not into it. "Gates of the Arctic is a wilderness park, with no roads or trails into the park lands." The Dalton Highway "parallels the eastern boundary of the park and it is possible to hike into the park from the road"; it is "a mostly unpaved, two lane industrial road, with no amenities or services between Fairbanks and Coldfoot."

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Gates of the Arctic National Park?
faq.a: It depends on the trip. The NPS: "Mid-June to September is usually the best time for backpacking and hiking"; July through August for float trips; "November through March is the best time for viewing the Aurora Borealis." Float plane service ends on September 23, and in May's break-up "the ice on the rivers is getting soft and mushy and starting to break apart."

faq.q: Does Gates of the Arctic National Park have a visitor center?
faq.a: Three, all outside the park. Bettles Ranger Station: "7 days a week, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., from July 1 to September 25". The Arctic Interagency Visitor Center at mile 175 of the Dalton Highway in Coldfoot, open daily in summer. The Fairbanks Alaska Public Lands Information Center: "7 days a week 8am-6 pm from May 25-September 11th". Anaktuvuk Pass also has a ranger station, staffed April to the end of September (anaktuvuk.htm).

faq.q: Can you camp in Gates of the Arctic National Park?
faq.a: Yes, anywhere suitable - there are no campgrounds. "There are no designated campsites in Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve." "Gravel bars make excellent campsites since they often have fewer mosquitoes than other sites"; "locate your camp well above current water levels." A certified bear-resistant food container "is required in all Alaskan parks", and the NPS recommends tent, cook area and container "all 100 yards apart in a triangle formation."

faq.q: Can you hunt in Gates of the Arctic National Park?
faq.a: Only in the preserve. "Sport hunting and trapping are permitted in Gates of the Arctic National Preserve, but not in Gates of the Arctic National Park." An Alaska State hunting licence is required for hunters 16 or older, under State regulations for Game Management Units 23, 24 and 26; guided hunts need an NPS Concession Contract or Commercial Use Authorization.

faq.q: What animals live in Gates of the Arctic National Park?
faq.a: The NPS names caribou ("Caribou trek from their boreal forest wintering grounds to their calving areas on the coastal plain"), grizzly and black bears, moose, Dall's sheep, muskox, lynx, beavers, snowshoe hares, arctic ground squirrels, lemmings and voles, wood frogs, arctic terns, ptarmigan and common loons; "Whitefish, northern pike and grayling feast in the rivers and lakes."

faq.q: How many acres is Gates of the Arctic National Park?
faq.a: 8.4 million acres. The park was "created to preserve and protect 8.4 million acres of the diverse arctic ecosystems of Alaska's central Brooks Range" and "serves as the headwaters for six Wild Rivers."

faq.q: Do people live in Gates of the Arctic National Park?
faq.a: Yes. "Situated inside the park's boundaries, at the top of a wide 2,100 foot mountain pass, the village of Anaktuvuk Pass is a great place to start your exploration of Gates of the Arctic." Its inhabitants are primarily inland Inupiat people who hunt caribou for subsistence; the Simon Paneak Memorial Museum has "Exhibits on Nunamiut history, life, and culture."

faq.q: Do you need tickets for Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve?
faq.a: No. "No entrance fees or registration are required to enter the park" and "An entrance pass is not required to access Gates Of The Arctic National Park & Preserve." Groups should contact the park several months ahead about permits, and the park asks visitors to attend a free backcountry orientation at a visitor center.

name: Kobuk Valley National Park
line: Arctic sand dunes and the caribou crossing

jewels.name: Great Kobuk Sand Dunes
jewels.booking_route: none needed - no entrance fee; reached by air taxi or flightseeing charter
jewels.blurb: "The largest active sand dunes in the Arctic": the Great Kobuk Sand Dunes cover "25 square miles of shifting, golden sand" and "Soaring dunes reach 100 feet into the air" - "a relic of the last Ice Age." "Aircraft on wheels can land right on the sand," and "Tents can be set up on any level surface." Near creeks, saturated sand "causes the sand to behave more like a liquid than a solid".

jewels.name: Western Arctic caribou migration
jewels.booking_route: none needed - wild animals on public land
jewels.blurb: "Twice a year, 250,000 caribou pass through Kobuk Valley National Park on their annual migration" - "the 600 mile trek between their summer and winter grounds". The park home page: "thousands of migrating caribou" cross the sculpted dunes.

jewels.name: Paatitaaq - Onion Portage
jewels.booking_route: none needed - reached by river or air taxi
jewels.blurb: "A stretch of river that has been the meeting ground for the Iñupiat, and their ancestors, for well over 8,000 years"; "A quarter of a million caribou migrate yearly across the Great Kobuk Sand Dunes", and the site is still a seasonal gathering place for the caribou harvest. "The story of Arctic archeology is dominated by one towering figure – J. Louis Giddings."

jewels.name: Kobuk River float, Ambler to Kiana
jewels.booking_route: none needed for independent travellers; organized recreational groups need a permit from the Chief Ranger
jewels.blurb: "The 380-mile-long river flows west to Kotzebue Sound, with 61 miles traversing Kobuk Valley National Park." "Starting in the village of Ambler, boating through the park and ending in the village of Kiana will take about 5-7 days." "Collapsible canoes and kayaks work especially well"; the dunes are "accessible from the river via a 2-3 mile hike across the tundra".

jewels.name: Little Kobuk and Hunt River Sand Dunes
jewels.blurb: Beside the main field lie "the smaller Little Kobuk Sand Dunes and Hunt River Sand Dunes"; together the dunes make "30 square miles of towering sand." When the glaciers retreated 14,000 years ago they "left behind 200,000 acres of rolling sand dunes."

jewels.name: Flightseeing over the park
jewels.booking_route: through an authorized air charter in Kotzebue or Bettles
jewels.blurb: "Hop aboard with Authorized charter companies out of Kotzebue or Bettles for a thrilling bird's-eye view of the park's landscape." Aircraft carry three to ten passengers by the hour or the day; day trips to the Great Kobuk Sand Dunes are popular. "Prices can vary, but on average they run $1000 per hour or more."

jewels.name: Northwest Arctic Heritage Center, Kotzebue
jewels.booking_route: none needed - free; PO Box 1029, Kotzebue, AK 99752; 907-318-2230
jewels.blurb: "The headquarters and primary visitor center for Western Arctic National Parklands": museum exhibits on Arctic ecology and Iñupiaq practices, films and ranger-led programs; (907) 318-2230. "The Northwest Arctic Heritage Center in Kotzebue is wheelchair accessible"; "a wheelchair is available upon request".

jewels.name: Kobuk Valley Junior Ranger programme
jewels.booking_route: none needed - free, by mail or in person
jewels.blurb: "Anyone can become a Kobuk Valley National Park Junior Ranger by printing a copy of the Western Arctic National Parklands Junior Ranger book, completing the activities and mailing the book back to the Northwest Arctic Heritage Center." Kids "can earn a Junior Ranger badge and a saber toothed tiger Junior Ranger patch"; the Heritage Center runs weekly summer kids' programs, (907) 318-2230.

jewels.name: Sheefish, grayling and pike fishing
jewels.booking_route: none needed in the park; an Alaska state fishing licence is required
jewels.blurb: "Sheefish, salmon, grayling, pike and Dolly Varden in the rivers are good to catch and good to eat." "The Pah, Black and Pick rivers are good for sheefish." "Anglers are required to have a fishing license and follow Alaska state fishing regulations." "Local subsistence users may be fishing with set nets - give them a wide berth".

jewels.name: Backcountry camping on the dunes and river
jewels.booking_route: none needed - no permit for independent travellers; organized groups need a Chief Ranger permit
jewels.blurb: "The most popular campsite is the Great Kobuk Sand Dunes". "There are also no designated campsites, and visitors must choose their own place to camp." The FAQ: "There are no accommodations or public facilities within the park. Backcountry camping is the only way to spend the night."

jewels.name: Midnight sun and northern lights
jewels.blurb: "The sun does not set between June 3rd and July 9th"; in winter "The sun is above the horizon only 1 ½ hours on December 21st". Northern lights are active year-round and best seen in winter's darkest nights.

jewels.name: Winter travel by ski, snow machine and dog team
jewels.blurb: The NPS lists winter activities - "snow machining, skiing and dog mushing" - for those with "Arctic winter survival skills". In winter, chartered aircraft may land on skis, and visitors bring their own skis, snowshoes, dog teams or snowmobiles.

jewels.name: Arctic tern and the summer birds
jewels.booking_route: none needed - wildlife on public land
jewels.blurb: The arctic tern flies "all the way from the coast of Antarctica - the longest migration of any bird in the world." "Ducks, cranes, loons, geese and swans" "make the valley their home for a few months each year." Grizzly bears, wolves and moose share the valley.

jewels.name: Mount Angayukaqsraq
jewels.blurb: The park's highest point: "Mount Angayukaqsraq – is 4760 feet high." "Kobuk" is an Inupiaq word meaning "big river", for the Kobuk River valley running through the park's center.

jewels.name: Bear-resistant food container, loaned free
jewels.booking_route: free loan at the Northwest Arctic Heritage Center; to own one, affiliate referral to BearVault (AvantLink)
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Animal-resistant food containers are available to borrow from the Northwest Arctic Heritage Center"; containers are loaned free, reserved by calling (907) 318-2230 no more than one month before the trip. "Keep your camp area clean and never bring food, even in the proper containers, into your tent."

jewels.name: Bear spray for the backcountry
jewels.blurb: NPS: bring "appropriate clothing, water and bear spray when you're hiking in the backcountry." The bear-safety page: "Stay Alert", "Be Visible & Make Noise", "Avoid Bears".

jewels.name: Rain gear, non-cotton layers and rubber boots
jewels.blurb: NPS: layers of "polypropylene, fleece, wool, or fur", "a breathable rain jacket and rain pants", sturdy hiking boots and "knee-high rubber/neoprene boots for wet terrain." "Avoid wearing clothing made of cotton." "Exposure and hypothermia are real threats to travelers."

jewels.name: Bug jackets, head nets and repellent
jewels.blurb: NPS: "Alaska is famous for mosquitoes, and for good reason, so carry bug protection when traveling in the park." Bug jackets, head nets and insect repellent are recommended, and black flies persist through fall.

jewels.name: Map, compass and GPS
jewels.blurb: The park has "no roads, trails, calculated mileages or specialized maps", so the NPS recommends "all visitors being prepared with map, compass, and GPS as well as the knowledge to use all three".

jewels.name: Gates of the Arctic and Kobuk Valley (Arctic Wild)
jewels.blurb: A 5-day guided base-camp trip from Kotzebue, "July 17-21, 2027", $9,100: two days on the Great Kobuk Sand Dunes - "The largest dune complex in the North American Arctic", with "sand ridges over 200 feet tall" - then two days in Gates of the Arctic. Includes round-trip airfare, wilderness meals, cooking equipment, base camp tent and professional guides. Booked by Reservation Request form and deposit.

jewels.name: Alaska's Northern National Parks: Krusenstern, Kobuk, Gates (Arctic Wild)
jewels.booking_route: own website Reservation Request form and deposit; 907.479.8203
jewels.blurb: A 7-day guided trip from Kotzebue, "July 5-11, 2027", $10,200: "The Great Kobuk Dunes are like the Sahara but with wolves, moose, and cranes" - 2.5 days on the dunes and at the Onion Portage archaeological sites, then Gates of the Arctic and Cape Krusenstern, where "limestone hills meet the cold Arctic Ocean". Includes round-trip airfare from Kotzebue, meals, camping equipment and guides.

jewels.name: Brooks Range Aviation Gates and Kobuk flight tour, Bettles
jewels.blurb: From Bettles, the Gates of the Arctic and Kobuk Valley package "typically lasts 4 to 5 hours", with "a landing either directly on the Kobuk dunes—or on the river just north of it" - "the largest active dune field above the Arctic Circle in North America." Per person: $1,995 for two passengers down to $1,595 for six. Bettles 907-692-5444 (June-September), Fairbanks 907-474-0595 (year-round).

jewels.name: Golden Eagle Outfitters, Kotzebue
jewels.blurb: "Experience the thrill of flightseeing in areas that most tours can't reach": custom flightseeing and air-taxi drop-off and pick-up from Kotzebue or Delta Junction, year round; flights to Kobuk Valley from Kotzebue, with popular 4-hour trips including a short landing. "All trips are custom and are a per-hour rate based on the aircraft. Call or email for a quote." Kotzebue 907-388-5968.

jewels.name: Bering Air, Kotzebue hub
jewels.booking_route: own website flight schedule and contact page
jewels.blurb: "Bering Air provides all of your air transportation solutions for Alaska and beyond" - scheduled service, statewide charter and helicopters from Nome, Kotzebue and Unalakleet, "Since 1979". From Kotzebue it serves the Kobuk River villages of Ambler, Kiana, Kobuk, Noorvik and Shungnak. Travel Alaska: "Call Bering Air for a flightseeing trip up the Kobuk River and to the far-flung villages along the way."

jewels.name: Wright Air Service, Fairbanks
jewels.blurb: "Proudly Serving Alaska Since 1966", with daily scheduled service to "more than 40 Interior and northern villages" and charters "to most locations in Alaska, including National Parks." Brooks Range Aviation points Bettles-bound travellers to Wright Air Service. Reservations (907) 474-0502.

jewels.name: Northwest Alaska Backcountry Rentals, Kotzebue
jewels.booking_route: not stated on the page read
jewels.blurb: Travel Alaska's local guide to Kotzebue: "Rent a kayak or raft from Northwest Alaska Backcountry Rentals." No rates, address or own website were found in this build.

jewels.name: Bettles Lodge
jewels.blurb: "Serving the Arctic Traveler since 1950" in Bettles, "35 miles north of the Arctic Circle" - "the 'jumping off' point of adventure into the Brooks Mountain Range, Gates of the Arctic National Park & Preserve, Noatak National Preserve, and Kobuk Valley National Park." "We offer unguided or guided wilderness trips including fishing, backpacking, canoe & rafting, photography and flight-seeing." 1-907-692-5111.

jewels.name: Nullaġvik Hotel, Kotzebue
jewels.blurb: "The Nullaġvik Hotel is more than a place to sleep. This is a gathering place to reflect, to rest, to meet and to dine in Kotzebue, the thriving hub of Northwest Alaska." "Owned by NANA, the Iñupiat People of the Northwest Arctic. Managed by NMS." Alaska.org: "71 guests rooms and 7 suites", an observation room overlooking the Sound and a restaurant.

jewels.name: Nullaġvik Hotel restaurant
jewels.blurb: The hotel's restaurant "offers delicious food and fantastic views" over Kotzebue Sound (alaska.org). Its own dining page refused the fetch (403), so hours and menu are not stated here.

jewels.name: Bayside Inn and Restaurant, Kotzebue
jewels.blurb: Anchorage Daily News review dated 9 November 2009: at 330 Shore Ave. overlooking Kotzebue Sound, "a small arm of the Chukchi Sea", serving "Chinese-American fare", with an upper-level lounge for hotel guests; 907-442-3600. The review is 2009 - its hours are not carried here and current opening was not confirmed in this build.

jewels.name: Kotzebue, the gateway on Kotzebue Sound
jewels.booking_route: none needed - a town; scheduled flights from Anchorage
jewels.blurb: Travel Alaska: the park is "75 miles east of Kotzebue", reached by "Air taxi from Kotzebue or Bettles". The local guide: "In early June, skip bedtime at the Nullaġvik Hotel and take a walk along Front Street"; "In July and August, nets will be set off the beach and we'll be fishing for salmon."

jewels.name: Sulianich Art Gallery, Kotzebue
jewels.blurb: "Stop in at the Sulianich Art Gallery. Local and Alaska Native art festoons the walls and display cases." The NPS describes the Sulianjich Art Center as "a nonprofit organization that markets the work of Northwest Alaskan artists."

jewels.name: Kobuk 440 sled dog race
jewels.booking_route: none needed - a public race start
jewels.blurb: "Teams from around the state come north to compete in the Kobuk 440, a dog sled race that begins with a mass start here on the ice in front of the post office." No dated edition was read in this build.

jewels.name: Alaska Geographic bookstore, Kotzebue
jewels.blurb: "Walk a block north and check out the Northwest Arctic Heritage Center and Alaska Geographic bookstore." Maps and park books sit beside the park's own visitor center.

jewels.name: Cape Krusenstern National Monument
jewels.booking_route: none needed - public land; reached by air charter from Kotzebue
jewels.blurb: From Kotzebue: "Muskoxen make their home along the coast and on the barren rounded mountains of Cape Krusenstern National Monument." Arctic Wild's 7-day Northern National Parks trip pairs it with Kobuk Valley.

jewels.name: Bettles, the Brooks Range gateway
jewels.booking_route: none needed - a village; scheduled flights from Fairbanks
jewels.blurb: A small village on the Koyukuk River in the Brooks Range foothills, "35 miles north of the Arctic Circle" - one of the two towns where, the NPS says, Kobuk Valley's air taxi offices are located. Brooks Range Aviation recommends "spending a night in Bettles" before a park flight.

faq.q: How do you get to Kobuk Valley National Park?
faq.a: By plane. The NPS: "There are no roads to provide access, so planes take care of most transportation needs." Commercial airlines serve Anchorage to Kotzebue and Fairbanks to Bettles, and from those towns visitors use "authorized air taxis" to reach the park.

faq.q: Can you drive to Kobuk Valley National Park?
faq.a: No. "Kobuk Valley National Park is very remote. There are no roads to provide access, so planes take care of most transportation needs."

faq.q: What is the best time to visit Kobuk Valley National Park?
faq.a: For floating the river the NPS says "July, August and early September are preferable"; June and July bring the peak of the mosquitoes.

faq.q: Where do you stay in Kobuk Valley National Park?
faq.a: In a tent. "There are no accommodations or public facilities within the park. Backcountry camping is the only way to spend the night."

faq.q: How many acres is Kobuk Valley National Park?
faq.a: "Of the approximately 1.7 million acres comprising Kobuk Valley National Park, approximately 190,000 acres were designated as wilderness."

faq.q: When was Kobuk Valley National Park established?
faq.a: It was a "National Monument - December 1, 1978" and became a "National Park - December 2, 1980".

faq.q: Does Kobuk Valley National Park have a visitor center?
faq.a: Yes, in Kotzebue: the Northwest Arctic Heritage Center is "the headquarters and primary visitor center for Western Arctic National Parklands", with exhibits, films and ranger-led programs; (907) 318-2230.

faq.q: How big are the Kobuk Valley National Park sand dunes?
faq.a: "The largest active sand dunes in the Arctic": the Great Kobuk Sand Dunes cover "25 square miles of shifting, golden sand", and with the Little Kobuk and Hunt River dunes the fields total "30 square miles of towering sand." "Aircraft on wheels can land right on the sand."

faq.q: When is the caribou migration in Kobuk Valley National Park?
faq.a: Spring and fall: "Twice a year, 250,000 caribou pass through Kobuk Valley National Park on their annual migration", on "the 600 mile trek between their summer and winter grounds".

faq.q: How much does it cost to go to Kobuk Valley National Park?
faq.a: The park itself is free - it "does not have an entrance gate, nor does it collect any fees to travel or camp in the park." The cost is the aircraft: the NPS says flightseeing charters "on average they run $1000 per hour or more."

name: Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park
line: The summit of Kīlauea, erupting in episodes inside Halemaʻumaʻu since December 2024, with a road down to the sea, a lit lava tube and a rainforest village at the gate

jewels.name: Kīlauea eruption viewing, Crater Rim Drive
jewels.booking_route: none needed - park entrance pass only
jewels.blurb: an episodic lava-fountaining eruption inside Halemaʻumaʻu since December 23, 2024 ("more than 50 eruptions"), seen from Uēkahuna, Kīlauea Overlook, Kūpinaʻi Pali and Keanakākoʻi; the eruption area is closed; lots typically fill by 10 a.m.; USGS: "relatively quiet" on 2026-10-01

jewels.name: Welcome Center
jewels.blurb: the temporary stand-in for Kīlauea Visitor Center during its renovation, 1.25 miles beyond the entrance station, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. daily, with the daily schedule of ranger-led activities and a Hawaiʻi Pacific Parks Association store

jewels.name: Chain of Craters Road
jewels.blurb: "18.8 miles (30.3 km) to the end of the road" down Kīlauea to the sea, with Maunaulu and Puʻuloa stops; no food, water or fuel; vault toilets at Maunaulu and road's end; NPS: "Do not feed nēnē"

jewels.name: Nāhuku (Thurston Lava Tube)
jewels.blurb: a lava tube about 500 years old in rainforest, 1.5 miles round trip from Kīlauea Iki Overlook, lit 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.; parking "extremely limited"; NPS hazards: rockfall, low ceilings, standing water

jewels.name: Kīlauea Iki Trail
jewels.blurb: a 3.3-mile loop from the overlook, 2 to 3 hours, "Steep and rocky, descent & ascent 400 feet" through rainforest onto a crater floor; overlook parking "extremely limited"

jewels.name: Puʻuloa Petroglyphs
jewels.blurb: 1.4 miles round trip across a 500-550-year-old lava field from Chain of Craters Road to "approximately 23,000 petroglyphs", viewed from a boardwalk

jewels.name: Summit day hikes: Devastation Trail, Haʻakulamanu (Sulphur Banks), Halemaʻumaʻu Trail, Kīpukapuaulu
jewels.blurb: the NPS list runs from Devastation's paved path to Haʻakulamanu, "where volcanic gases have deposited colorful crystals", the Halemaʻumaʻu Trail "down to the floor of Kīlauea caldera" and the Kīpukapuaulu botanical loop

jewels.name: Kahuku Unit, Kaʻū
jewels.blurb: the park's ranching-history unit near mile-marker 70.5 on Highway 11, open Thursday to Sunday 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., eight trails from 0.4 to 7 miles round trip including the Glover Trail to a pit-crater rim; no potable water

jewels.name: Backcountry permits and the eight wilderness sites
jewels.booking_route: Recreation.gov; Backcountry Office in person 8 a.m.-4 p.m.
jewels.blurb: Kaʻaha, Halapē, Keauhou, ʻĀpua Point, Nāpau, Pepeiao Cabin, Red Hill Cabin and Mauna Loa Cabin; $10 a trip for up to 12 people and 7 nights; 75% of permits online up to 90 days ahead, 25% in person at the Backcountry Office

jewels.name: Volcano House
jewels.blurb: the park's lodge on Crater Rim Drive, "33 historic guest rooms, a dining room, snack bar, lounge, and gift shop, along with cultural events", run by Hawai'i Volcanoes Lodge Company LLC

jewels.name: The Rim at Volcano House
jewels.blurb: breakfast buffet, lunch and dinner with the Kīlauea caldera and Halemaʻumaʻu as backdrop and live local music; a Certified Green Restaurant; dinner reservations required

jewels.name: Friends of Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park (Institute field seminars and private tours)
jewels.blurb: the park's official philanthropic partner runs field seminars, private tours, monthly Sunday Walks in the Park, an October 17 artist residency conversation and Holidays in Kahuku on December 5, 2026

jewels.name: Nāmakanipaio Campground and camper cabins
jewels.blurb: tent and RV camping at 4,000 feet under eucalyptus and ʻōhiʻa, 26 sites per Hipcamp ($20 a night, $15 with a park pass); Volcano House manages "10 newly refurbished camper cabins and campsites" here

jewels.name: Kulanaokuaiki Campground
jewels.booking_route: not observed (the NPS campground page loaded with its reservation section empty)
jewels.blurb: an 8-site tent and RV campground inside the park, "~5 miles down Hulina [sic] Pali Road" per Hipcamp, "new campground with two wheelchair accessible sites", toilets and picnic tables

jewels.name: The Tranquil Homestead, Mountain View
jewels.blurb: an off-grid tiny-home cabin for up to four in a rainbow-eucalyptus rainforest, with ducks and peafowl to feed, full kitchen and composting toilet; 100% recommend

jewels.name: Sunrise Cabanas Panoramic Views, Nāʻālehu
jewels.blurb: two octagonal coastal cabanas and a campsite on a "100% solar powered" permaculture farm with "over 100 varieties of tropical fruits", looking to Mauna Loa, Kīlauea and the Kaʻū coast; Nāʻālehu is inside the Hurricane Lala advisory area

jewels.name: Paradise Yurts, Nāʻālehu
jewels.blurb: a private yurt for two on 12 acres of citrus, avocado, breadfruit and banana, with outdoor rain shower and farm breakfast daily; Star Host, 100% recommend; Nāʻālehu is inside the Hurricane Lala advisory area

jewels.name: Rainbow's End Farm & Homestead
jewels.blurb: off-grid, solar-powered glamping on hand-cleared land with "fancy forts"; 2 sites, 97% of 135 reviews recommend

jewels.name: Yip Camp and Eco-Retreat Center, Fern Forest
jewels.blurb: an off-grid 3-acre rainforest retreat at about 2,700 feet on Kīlauea with canvas glamping tents, a 140 sq ft loft cabin, tent sites and two no-hookup RV sites; solar power, rainwater catchment, fire pit

jewels.name: Ember & Fern Retreat
jewels.blurb: three "traditional Hawaiian style homes" on rainwater-harvested land, cabin glamping with showers and WiFi; 99% of 39 reviews recommend

jewels.name: Coco Hut Glamping at Honua La'a, Road to the Sea, Kaʻū
jewels.blurb: two glamping cabins on 19 acres with access to a remote green sand beach 4 miles away; pets allowed, campfires

jewels.name: Road to the Sea Glamping, Kaʻū
jewels.blurb: "beautiful furnished cabins" on 20 off-grid acres; pets allowed, showers; 96% of 28 reviews recommend

jewels.name: Moon Garden Getaway, Mountain View
jewels.blurb: tent, RV and glamping on a Star Host farm with volleyball, frisbee golf and tetherball; 99% of 350 reviews recommend

jewels.name: The Kikala Waterfall Lodge, Hilo area
jewels.blurb: four cabin and glamping sites on "14 acres of riverfront Cloud forest" with a Zendo meditation space

jewels.name: The Bali Hale, Puna
jewels.blurb: a screened glamping bungalow on a secluded half-acre with a yoga platform; 99% of 58 reviews recommend

jewels.name: Farm to Table Hawaii, Hilo area
jewels.blurb: tents, a dome and a tiny home on a farm offering "farm-to-table meals" and "cooking classes" with Chef Justine Ma

jewels.name: Camp South Pt Green/Blacksand Beach, Waiʻōhinu
jewels.blurb: a 22-acre property with RV/tent sites, group camping for 25 and two rooms, potable water and hot showers, "easy access to Southpoint, Greensand and Blacksand Beaches"; Waiʻōhinu is inside the Hurricane Lala advisory area

jewels.name: Hawaii Island's Best Campsites (Hawaii Island Resort), Nāʻālehu
jewels.blurb: five dispersed RV, van and tent sites in an 8-acre macadamia orchard with hot showers and a heated saltwater pool with water slide; Hipcamp 2023 "Best in Hawaii: 3rd place"; Nāʻālehu is inside the Hurricane Lala advisory area

jewels.name: Papa's Hawaiian Orchid Farm, Pāhoa
jewels.blurb: a tent and RV site on a "commercial orchid farm" with a "lava tube on the property"; 98% of 390 reviews recommend

jewels.name: Hawaii Forest & Trail - Volcano Direct Hiking Adventure
jewels.blurb: a 10-hour guided day into the park with naturalist guides, lunch and all gear, adults from $259, departing Kona weekly with Waikoloa and Hilo pickups; the operator cites "a continuous commercial operating permit for over three decades"

jewels.name: KapohoKine Adventures, Hilo
jewels.blurb: volcano tours, ziplines and ATV from the Grand Naniloa lobby on Banyan Drive; the Evening Volcano Explorer from Waikoloa/Kohala runs about 11 hours with dinner ($229, listed down from $295.99)

jewels.name: Paradise Helicopters
jewels.blurb: helicopter tours from Hilo and Kona airports, with a "Hawaii Lava Update" on its site; tour names and prices for Kīlauea flights were not shown on the pages loaded

jewels.name: Blue Hawaiian Helicopters, Hilo and Waikoloa
jewels.blurb: Discover Hilo (50 min, from $439) over "newly formed volcanic landscapes", Big Island Spectacular from Waikoloa (1 hr 45 min, from $719), and Waterfalls and Volcano by Air and Land (8 hours, from $1,009) with ground time at Kīlauea

jewels.name: Volcano Winery
jewels.booking_route: walk-in for tastings; tours need 24 hours' advance booking, engine not observed; (808) 967-7772
jewels.blurb: a Volcano winery pouring grape wines, fruit blends and honey meads with estate teas and Kaʻū coffee; $20 six-pour tastings daily 12-5 p.m., Aliʻi Vineyard Tour $40, Wine Maker's Tour $75, Kilauea Ki tea presentation $60

jewels.name: Kilauea Lodge and Restaurant, Volcano Village
jewels.booking_route: own site (reservations.kilauealodge.com) for rooms; dining engine not observed; (808) 967-7366
jewels.blurb: a small lodge of about 12 rooms at 19-3948 Old Volcano Road with an outdoor jacuzzi, tropical garden and an on-property restaurant serving "fresh, locally sourced dishes"

jewels.name: Volcano Garden Arts and Café Ono, Volcano Village
jewels.booking_route: walk-in; Volcano Artist Cottage via volcanoartistcottage.net
jewels.blurb: a gallery of contemporary Hawaiian art, ceramics and sculpture in a redwood farmhouse on "the 1908 Hopper Estate" at 19-3834 Old Volcano Road; gallery daily 10-4 except Wednesday, Café Ono Thursday-Sunday 11-2

jewels.name: Hilo Farmers Market
jewels.blurb: daily 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. at Kamehameha Avenue and Mamo Street in historic downtown Hilo, with "tropical fruits, exotic flowers, handcrafted art, and authentic Hawaiian treats"

jewels.name: Mauna Loa Macadamia Nut Visitor Center, Keaʻau
jewels.blurb: free macadamia samples and dairy-free ice cream, a self-guided nature walk of 25+ plant and animal species, and products from 25+ local makers at 16-701 Macadamia Road; Monday-Saturday 9-4, closed Sundays; open on the date of this build

jewels.name: Hilo Coffee Mill, Mountain View
jewels.booking_route: walk-in; farm tours not shown on the page
jewels.blurb: mill and café at 17-997 Volcano Road on the Hilo-Volcano highway, "Hawai'i's favorite island coffee supplier since 2001"; open 8:30-3 Tuesday-Sunday, 9-3 Monday

jewels.name: Kaʻū Coffee Mill, Pāhala
jewels.blurb: a Kaʻū coffee and macadamia producer at 96-2694 Wood Valley Road; the site states "Tours are not currently available due to road damage"

jewels.name: Punaluʻu Bake Shop, Nāʻālehu
jewels.blurb: "The Southernmost Bakery in the U.S.A.", known for Hawaiian sweet bread and malasadas; on the date of this build the shop, visitor centre and online store are "temporarily closed due to damage from Hurricane Lala"

jewels.name: ʻImiloa Astronomy Center, Hilo
jewels.blurb: Polynesian navigation and Maunakea astronomy with Hawaiʻi Island's only planetarium, at 600 ʻImiloa Place on the UH Hilo campus; Tuesday-Sunday 9-4:30

jewels.name: Hilo's gardens and falls: Liliʻuokalani Gardens and Waiānuenue (Rainbow Falls)
jewels.blurb: per the state tourism site, a 30-acre Japanese garden with fishponds and pagodas, and the 80-foot Rainbow Falls in Wailuku River State Park; the Pacific Tsunami Museum is downtown

jewels.name: Lava Tree State Monument, Puna
jewels.blurb: a 17.1-acre state monument with "a forest of lava trees along an 0.7 mile loop trail", daily during daylight, no fee; the state notes some Hawaiʻi island parks are still affected by hurricane recovery

jewels.name: Kalapana and Pāhoa, Puna
jewels.blurb: per the state tourism site, Kaimū and Kalapana were engulfed by Kīlauea lava in 1990; Uncle Robert's ʻAwa Bar and Farmer's Market stands by the flow, and Pāhoa is "a former mill town with an inviting boardwalk" with the weekend Makuʻu Farmers Market nearby

jewels.name: Volcano Village
jewels.blurb: per the state tourism site, a "charming artist community located five minutes from Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park"; the Cooper Center, "the heartbeat of the Volcano Village Community", sits here (its farmers market schedule did not load)

faq.q: Is Kīlauea erupting right now?
faq.a: As of October 1, 2026, USGS states that an episodic lava fountaining eruption has been occurring in Halemaʻumaʻu crater since December 23, 2024, and that Kīlauea was relatively quiet that day. The NPS counts more than 50 eruptive episodes since December 2024. Activity comes in episodes with pauses between them, so lava on any given day is not certain.

faq.q: Where can I see the eruption from?
faq.a: The NPS names Uēkahuna, Kīlauea Overlook at Kūkamāhuākea (Steam Vents), Kūpinaʻi Pali and Keanakākoʻi along Crater Rim Drive. The eruption area itself is closed to the public, and parking lots typically fill by 10 a.m.

faq.q: How much is the entrance fee?
faq.a: $30 per private vehicle, $25 per motorcycle and $15 per person on foot or bicycle (16 and over). The park does not accept cash.

faq.q: Is the Kīlauea Visitor Center open?
faq.a: No. The NPS says KVC, its restrooms, sidewalk, lānai and about half its parking are closed for renovation from February 18, 2025 to late 2026. The Welcome Center, 1.25 miles beyond the entrance station, stands in, open 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. daily.

faq.q: Can I camp in the park?
faq.a: Yes. Volcano House manages camper cabins and campsites at Nāmakanipaio, Kulanaokuaiki is a second campground, and eight backcountry sites are available on a $10 permit booked through Recreation.gov up to 90 days ahead.

faq.q: How far is the park from Hilo and Kona?
faq.a: The NPS gives 30 miles from Hilo (about 45 minutes) and 95 miles from Kailua-Kona on Highway 11 (2 to 2.5 hours).

hero.query: Hawai'i Volcanoes National Park, Hawai'i

name: Haleakalā National Park
line: A 10,023-foot summit sacred to Native Hawaiians, a sunrise you reserve 60 days out for $1, a cinder crater you can sleep in, and a second district on the rainforest coast twelve miles past Hāna

jewels.name: Haleakalā sunrise (reservation required, 3-7 a.m.)
jewels.booking_route: Recreation.gov only (calling the park or visiting in person cannot secure one); $1.00 per vehicle plus the entrance fee
jewels.blurb: "In order to view sunrise at Haleakalā National Park, you will need to make a reservation ahead of time" for the 3:00 AM - 7:00 AM window; released "up to 60 days in advance" at 7:00 am HST plus a portion "2 days (48 hours) in advance"; "A visitor may only purchase one sunrise reservation per three-day period"; NPS: "Weather immediately before dawn and immediately after dusk are regularly wet, windy, and below freezing."

jewels.name: The summit: Haleakalā Visitor Center and Pā Kaʻoao
jewels.booking_route: none needed outside 3-7 a.m. - entrance pass only
jewels.blurb: a 0.4-mile, 100-ft walk "up the puʻu next to Haleakalā Visitor Center to view ancient rock wall shelters and the crater"; the park store there is open "daily from sunrise - 12:00 pm"; NPS: "Please be quiet and respectful. The summit is sacred to Native Hawaiians."

jewels.name: Keoneheʻeheʻe (Sliding Sands) Trail
jewels.blurb: "Hike downhill into the crater": 0.5 mile round trip to the first overlook, the crater floor 3.9 miles down about 2,500 feet below, 11 miles as a full day across to the Halemauʻu Trail; the NPS rule is to allow twice the time to hike out

jewels.name: Halemauʻu Trail
jewels.blurb: "Hike on a rocky path to a crater viewpoint": 2.2 miles round trip, 1.1 miles to the viewpoint, 400 ft, past the "Rainbow Bridge" natural land bridge; also the route to Hōlua cabin and campsite (3.7 miles one way)

jewels.name: Supply Trail
jewels.blurb: 4.6 miles round trip, 975 ft, "Hike to the junction with the Halemauʻu Trail"

jewels.name: Leleiwi Overlook
jewels.blurb: "Short walk to a crater viewpoint", 0.30 mile round trip, 100 ft - the shortest crater view on the NPS trail list

jewels.name: Hosmer Grove trail
jewels.blurb: a 0.54-mile loop, 50 ft: "Compare non-native trees and native shrubland. View honeycreepers found nowhere else on earth."

jewels.name: Hosmer Grove Campground
jewels.blurb: "Six designated sites" in an open grassy area "at nearly 7,000 feet (2134m)" with picnic table, grill and potable water; $20 a night, three-night maximum; NPS: "Come prepared for rain and cold weather!"

jewels.name: Wilderness cabins: Hōlua, Kapalaoa, Palikū
jewels.booking_route: Recreation.gov or 1-877-444-6777, up to six months ahead
jewels.blurb: three historic crater cabins, "12 padded bunks" each, wood-burning and propane stoves, pit toilets and water nearby, "no electricity"; Hōlua 3.7 mi via Halemauʻu, Kapalaoa 5.6 mi and Palikū 9.3 mi via Keoneheʻeheʻe; $75 a night, three nights maximum; NPS: "not checked by NPS staff daily"

jewels.name: Wilderness tent camping: Hōlua and Palikū
jewels.booking_route: Recreation.gov only, up to six months ahead
jewels.blurb: two hike-in primitive sites, $20 a night, five people and two tents a site (group sites ten and four), water "must be filtered or treated before drinking"; "There is no cell phone service in Haleakalā Crater"

jewels.name: Stargazing at the summit
jewels.blurb: NPS advice: "Turn off all white lights (including phones!)"; use red lights "only when necessary"; "the temperature can drop quickly when the sun goes down!" - bring a hat, coat, long pants and warm shoes; overnight stays only in designated campgrounds

jewels.name: ʻĀhinahina (Haleakalā silversword)
jewels.blurb: found on the "aeolian desert cinder slopes of the crater"; "Silverswords live between 3 and 90 years or more" and flower once, then die; once "ripped up and taken home by visitors as souvenirs", they "now depend on management efforts for survival" - stay on trails

jewels.name: Kīpahulu District and Visitor Center
jewels.blurb: the park's coastal district, reached "12 miles beyond Hāna", with "views of waterfalls, sweeping ocean vistas, and Hawaiian cultural experiences"; "inhabited by native people for hundreds of years and remains an integral part of a thriving culture"; Kīpahulu Visitor Center park store daily 9:00 - 5:00

jewels.name: Pīpīwai Trail
jewels.blurb: 4 miles round trip, 800 ft, "Moderately strenuous", "through a freshwater stream and diverse forest areas with views of waterfalls"; NPS: "Flash floods and sudden rock falls can occur at any time! Entry and wading in the streams is not recommended."

jewels.name: Kūloa Point Trail and the Pools of ʻOheʻo
jewels.blurb: 0.5 mile, 80 ft, "past a Hawaiian cultural demonstration area to Kuloa Point" with "beautiful ocean views and archaeological sites"; NPS status: "The Pools of ʻOheʻo in the Kīpahulu District are not accessible for swimming. The pools can be viewed safely from the Kūloa Point Trail."

jewels.name: Kīpahulu Campground
jewels.blurb: "20 sites total including 5 walk-in sites, 15 drive-in sites, and 1 group drive-in site" above the ocean; $20 a night, three-night maximum; "No water is available at the Kīpahulu Campground. There are no showers or electrical outlets" (water station at the visitor center); "Be prepared for rain, harsh sun, and mosquitoes"

jewels.name: Kīpahulu ʻOhana and Kapahu Living Farm
jewels.booking_route: contact form, (808) 248-8673; no schedule or price published
jewels.blurb: "a grassroots Hawaiian 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization founded in 1995" that manages Kapahu Living Farm, a traditional wetland taro farm in the Kīpahulu District, under a partnership agreement with the park; lists Cultural Interpretive Hike Tours and ʻĀina education work days

jewels.name: Haleakalā EcoTours
jewels.blurb: listed on its own site as a "Haleakala Park Authorized Concessioner"; Haleakalā Sunrise Tour "$230+ taxes & fees", Sunset Tour $250+, plus summit, rainforest and Road to Hāna tours with NAI-certified guides; departs 810 Haiku Rd, Haiku

jewels.name: Bike Maui (Haleakala Bike Company)
jewels.blurb: self-guided and guided downhill bike tours: Haleakala Sunrise self-guided $190, Morning $150, Express $79, guided sunrise $225, with discounts for bookings 72+ hours ahead; in-park portions run through sister company Haleakalā EcoTours; base at 810 Haiku Rd, Haiku

jewels.name: Maui Sunriders Bike Co., Pāʻia
jewels.blurb: "The original & most trusted self-guided bike tour experience for over 25 years. Ride at your own pace with full van support" - Haleakalā self-guided, guided and Bike & Brew tours, plus a North Shore e-bike tour; operating since 2001, 71 Baldwin Ave, Pāʻia

jewels.name: Pony Express Tours - Crater Junction Ride
jewels.blurb: horseback down the Sliding Sands Trail into the crater: about 4 hours, 7.5 miles round trip, "Descends 2,500 ft to crater floor" with a picnic lunch, $182 + tax, 8:30 a.m., prior riding experience recommended; shorter Haleakala Ranch Paniolo (2 hr, $110) and Mauka (1.5 hr, $95) rides at 4,000 feet

jewels.name: Surfing Goat Dairy, Kula
jewels.blurb: an "award-winning goat dairy farm" on Haleakalā's slopes at 3651 Omaopio Rd with a Daily Casual Tour, Baby Goat Interaction, the Golden Girl Experience (18+) and Evening Chores & Milking tours; Tuesday-Saturday 9:30-5

jewels.name: MauiWine, ʻUlupalakua
jewels.blurb: the Ulupalakua Vineyards tasting room at 14815 Piilani Hwy pouring estate wines, pineapple wines and the Rose Ranch collection, Tuesday-Sunday 11-5; the winery warns "GPS MAY ROUTE INCORRECTLY" and gives Highway 37 through Keokea

jewels.name: Ulupalakua Ranch Store & Grill
jewels.blurb: a working cattle ranch established in 1845, "one of Hawaii's largest working cattle ranches"; the grill serves "grass fed beef, venison, and elk burgers sourced right from the pastures", Tuesday-Sunday 11-4

jewels.name: Aliʻi Kula Lavender
jewels.blurb: a lavender farm at 1100 Waipoli Road, Kula, open Friday-Monday 10-4 (last entry 3:45), closed Tuesday-Thursday, with a gift shop and its "sustainable aloha" message

jewels.name: Kula Botanical Garden
jewels.blurb: a garden established in 1971 at 638 Kekaulike, Kula, "Open every day - 365 days a year", self-guided tours 9 to 3:15; adults $15, children 6-12 $5; Maui-grown Christmas trees in December

jewels.name: Oʻo Farm, Kula
jewels.blurb: "a scenic parcel of land in upcountry Maui above Kula, dedicated to culinary farming and agritourism" at 651 Waipoli Rd: a Coffee & Brunch Experience and a Farm-to-Table Lunch and Farmer Field Tour; "A tour reservation is mandatory to access the property"

jewels.name: Grandma's Coffee House, Keokea
jewels.blurb: a family coffee house at 9232 Kula Hwy whose story starts in 1918 when Grandma began roasting coffee; daily 7-2 with pumpkin bread, pineapple-coconut-macadamia muffins and "the best organic coffee around"; MauiWine routes visitors past it

jewels.name: Kula Bistro
jewels.blurb: breakfast (7:30-10:30, not Monday or Tuesday), lunch and dinner (11-8) at 4566 Lower Kula Road; "No Reservations, walk-ins only!"

jewels.name: Kula Lodge
jewels.blurb: vacation chalets with lanais and electric fireplaces at 15200 Haleakala Hwy (Route 377); on the date of this build "The main restaurant is closed indefinitely due to fire damage" while a food truck and the Kula Marketplace run 7 a.m.-7 p.m.

jewels.name: Kula Sandalwoods Inn
jewels.blurb: six hillside cottages at 3,300 feet at 15427 Haleakalā Hwy with "sweeping bi-coastal views of the islands of Moloka'i and Lana'i" and a breakfast-and-lunch café; "Native Hawaiian owned and operated"

jewels.name: Upcountry Farmers Market, Kulamalu
jewels.blurb: Saturdays 7-11 a.m. at 55 Kiopaa St (Kulamalu Town Center), "over 100 local vendors showcasing the best of Maui" - produce, flowers, fresh fish, baked goods and crafts

jewels.name: Hui Noʻeau Visual Arts Center, Makawao
jewels.booking_route: walk-in for gallery; classes via own site
jewels.blurb: a nonprofit arts centre founded in 1934 on the historic Kaluanui Estate at 2841 Baldwin Avenue, Tuesday-Saturday 9-4, with exhibitions, a Gallery Shop and classes from ceramics and glassblowing to Hawaiian arts

jewels.name: Kula
jewels.blurb: per the state tourism site, "In the heart of Upcountry Maui, Kula is a quaint, rustic area on the slopes of Haleakalā" - the farm and lodging belt on the summit road

jewels.name: Makawao
jewels.blurb: per the state tourism site, "Located on the mid-slopes of Maui's Haleakalā volcano, Makawao has one foot in its plantation past and another in its thriving arts community"

jewels.name: Pāʻia
jewels.blurb: per the state tourism site, "the historic town of Pāʻia on Maui's north coast"; the NPS names Pāʻia as the place to refuel for Kīpahulu, since there is no gas in the park

jewels.name: Mama's Fish House, Kūʻau
jewels.blurb: open since 1973 at 799 Poho Place overlooking Kūʻau Bay, fish from local fishing families, a 2018 James Beard Foundation semi-finalist; "books up months in advance", bookings up to 18 months out; The Inn at Mama's has beachfront lodging

jewels.name: Hāna
jewels.blurb: per the state tourism site, "A charming small town where time seems an abstract concept and aloha is a way of life"; the Pools of ʻOheʻo are "15 minutes south of Hāna on Highway 31"

jewels.name: Hana-Maui Resort, Destination by Hyatt
jewels.blurb: oceanfront bungalows, garden suites and villas at 5031 Hana Hwy where rooms "intentionally lack televisions and clocks"; Hana Ranch restaurant (farm-to-table, ocean-to-fork), Paniolo Bar, and a spa with lomi lomi

jewels.name: Hāna Farms
jewels.blurb: a farm stand, bakery ("banana bread and desserts daily") and The Bamboo Hale serving "wood-fired pizza" at 2910 Hana Highway, "after mile marker 31, just after the 'Welcome to Hāna' sign"; Friday hours run to 8 p.m.

jewels.name: Kahanu Garden and Piʻilanihale Heiau, Hāna
jewels.blurb: a National Tropical Botanical Garden site at 650 Ulaino Rd, home to Piʻilanihale Heiau and described as "a profound Hawaiian place"; self-guided and guided tours, "guided tours may sell out in advance"

jewels.name: Waiʻānapanapa State Park
jewels.blurb: "All visitors and commercial operators will need to make reservations to enter"; open 7-6; non-residents $5 a person and $10 a vehicle; an "ancient Hawaiian coastal trail which leads to Hana" and a heiau; tent camping $30 and cabins $100 a night

jewels.name: Wahi Nanea Place of Relaxation, Kula
jewels.blurb: six tent, RV and cabin sites at 2,800 feet with picnic tables, grill, fire pit and a shared gazebo; 97% of 912 reviews recommend

jewels.name: Lokalani Gardens
jewels.blurb: a "Remote, off-grid farm...surrounded by wild, untamed land" with two sites, medicinal plants and yoga sessions; one review on Hipcamp

jewels.name: Polipoli Spring State Recreation Area (closed)
jewels.booking_route: closed - not bookable on the date of this build
jewels.blurb: "Camping and lodging (one cabin) within the fog belt of the Kula Forest Reserve at 6200 foot elevation", four-wheel drive required; state notice 10/1/26: "Polipoli - remains CLOSED due to downed trees"

jewels.name: Hāna Lava Tube (Kaʻeleku Cave) (closed)
jewels.blurb: the site states "The cave has been temporarily closed by the government until further notice while they schedule an archaeological inventory survey of the cave"

faq.q: Do I need a reservation for Haleakalā sunrise?
faq.a: Yes. Entry between 3 and 7 a.m. requires a sunrise reservation made on Recreation.gov. They are released up to 60 days in advance at 7 a.m. HST, with a further portion released 48 hours ahead, and one visitor may buy only one per three-day period.

faq.q: How much does it cost to visit Haleakalā?
faq.a: $30 per private vehicle, $25 per motorcycle or $15 per person, plus $1.00 for a sunrise reservation if you are entering between 3 and 7 a.m. The park does not accept cash.

faq.q: How cold is it at the summit?
faq.a: The NPS says summit temperatures are at least 20 degrees colder than at sea level and often drop below freezing, and that weather just before dawn and after dusk is regularly wet, windy and below freezing.

faq.q: Can I swim at the Pools of ʻOheʻo?
faq.a: No. The NPS states the pools are not accessible for swimming and can be viewed from the Kūloa Point Trail. It warns that flash floods and sudden rock falls can occur at any time at Kīpahulu.

faq.q: Can I stay overnight inside the crater?
faq.a: Yes, in three wilderness cabins (Hōlua, Kapalaoa, Palikū) at $75 a night or two tent sites at $20 a night, all reserved on Recreation.gov up to six months ahead. There is no cell phone service in the crater.

faq.q: How long is the drive?
faq.a: The NPS gives about 2.5 hours from Kahului to the summit, 3 hours from Wailea, 3.5 from Lahaina, and about 4 hours from Kahului to Kīpahulu. There is no gas in the park; refuel in Pukalani or Pāʻia.

faq.q: Can I ride a bike down Haleakalā?
faq.a: Commercial downhill bike rides inside the park have been under an NPS moratorium since 2008, with bike companies authorized to run van tours within the park. Operators such as Bike Maui and Maui Sunriders sell downhill tours; check with them where the ride begins.

seo.meta_title: Haleakalā National Park: Sunrise Reservations, Crater Trails & Kīpahulu | TravelWell
seo.meta_description: The $1 sunrise reservation, Sliding Sands and the crater cabins, Pīpīwai at Kīpahulu, and the Upcountry farms, wine and stays from Kula to Hāna.
